e1/speaking-listening/docs/task3-describ: Describe the Photo: E1 and E2 Model Scripts Oct 12, 2026 · @Atin Model answers for Task 3 of the ESB Speaking and Listening exam. In each script, every question picks up a word from the line just before it, so a cut-up version only fits together one way. Entry 1 script E1 Task 3 (4 minutes): the examiner gives each learner one photo. The learner describes it, then answers questions about their opinion. Photos: Amina’s photo shows a busy fruit market with a smiling stallholder in a green hat. Hassan’s photo shows a park with a woman walking a small brown dog, a big tree, and two old men on a bench. Examiner: Now we are going to look at some photos. Amina, here is your photo. Please tell me what you can see. Amina: In this photo I can see a market. There are a lot of people. Examiner: What are the people doing? Amina: They are buying fruit. Examiner: What fruit can you see? Amina: I can see bananas and oranges. A man is selling them. Examiner: What is the man wearing? Amina: He is wearing a green hat. He is smiling. Examiner: Why is he smiling, do you think? Amina: Because the market is very busy. He is selling a lot. Examiner: Do you like busy places like this? Amina: Yes, I do. I like busy markets because the food is cheap. Examiner: Which market do you go to? Amina: I go to Ridley Road Market. It is near my house. Examiner: Thank you, Amina. Now, Hassan, here is your photo. What can you see? Hassan: In this photo I can see a park. There is a woman with a dog. Examiner: What is the woman doing? Hassan: She is walking her dog. They are next to a big tree. Examiner: What is under the tree? Hassan: There is a bench under the tree. Two old men are sitting on it. Examiner: What are the two men doing? Hassan: They are talking. It looks very quiet. Examiner: Do you like quiet places? Hassan: Yes, I do. I like quiet parks because I can relax. Examiner: Is there a quiet park near your home? Hassan: Yes, there is. I go to London Fields on Sundays. Examiner: Thank you, Hassan. That is the end of this task. Entry 2 script E2 Task 3 (4 minutes): the examiner gives each learner two photos. The learner describes them, answers follow-up questions, and compares the two photos. Photos: Amina gets (1) a crowded train station in the morning, people looking at their phones, and (2) a quiet village road, a man on a bike, no cars. Hassan gets (1) a family of five having dinner at home, and (2) friends laughing at a birthday meal in a restaurant, with a cake on the table. Examiner: In this task you will each describe two photos. Amina, here are your photos. Please describe the first one. Amina: In the first photo I can see a train station. It is very crowded. Examiner: Why is it so crowded, do you think? Amina: I think it is the morning and people are going to work. Many people are looking at their phones. Examiner: Why are they looking at their phones? Amina: Maybe they are checking the train times. I think the trains are late. Examiner: Have you ever had a problem with a late train? Amina: Yes. Last week my train was thirty minutes late, so I was late for college. Examiner: Oh dear. Now, Amina, please describe your second photo. Amina: In the second photo there is a quiet road in the countryside. A man is riding a bike. There are no cars. Examiner: Why are there no cars, do you think? Amina: Because it is far from the city. It is a small village road. Examiner: So, how is the village different from the station in your first photo? Amina: The station is much busier and noisier than the village. The village is more relaxing. Examiner: Which place do you like more, the station or the village? Amina: I like the village more because it is more relaxing. But I live in the city because my college is here. Examiner: Thank you, Amina. Hassan, here are your two photos. Please describe the first one. Hassan: In the first photo a family is having dinner at home. There are five people at the table. Examiner: What are they eating for dinner? Hassan: They are eating rice and chicken. I think the mother cooked it. Examiner: Do you cook for your family? Hassan: Yes, I cook every evening. Yesterday I made lentil soup. Examiner: That sounds delicious. Hassan, now describe your second photo. Hassan: In the second photo some friends are eating in a restaurant. They are all laughing. Examiner: What do you think is so funny? Hassan: Maybe one friend is telling a joke. I think it is a birthday party, because there is a cake on the table. Examiner: How do you celebrate birthdays? Hassan: We usually have a big meal at home with my family. Examiner: So, how is eating at home different from eating in a restaurant? Hassan: Eating at home is cheaper than a restaurant. But a restaurant is easier, because you don’t cook or wash up. Examiner: Which do you like more, eating at home or in a restaurant? Hassan: I like eating at home more, because the food is healthier. Examiner: Thank you, Hassan. That is the end of this task.

Questions 4–5 on each page are personal. 1. In the kitchen Part 1: 1 kitchen, 2 cooking, 3 red, 4 three, 5 apples, 6 cat, 7 chair Model: In this picture I can see a kitchen. A woman is cooking. She has a red top. There are three green apples on the table. A black cat is on the chair. I like cooking because it is relaxing. Part 3: 1) A: The woman's top is red. B: The woman's top is green. 2) A: There are three apples. B: There are two apples. 3) A: The cat is black. B: The cat is orange. 4) A: It is three o'clock. B: It is six o'clock. 5) A: It is sunny. B: It is cloudy. 2. In the park Part 1: 1 park, 2 sunny, 3 walking, 4 dog, 5 children, 6 football, 7 bird Model: In this picture I can see a park. It is sunny. A man is walking his dog. Two children are playing football. There is a bird in the tree. I like parks because they are green and quiet. Part 3: 1) A: The man's jacket is blue. B: The man's jacket is red. 2) A: The dog is brown. B: The dog is black. 3) A: There is a bird in the tree. B: There is no bird in the tree. 4) A: There are no apples in the tree. B: There are apples in the tree. 5) A: The girl's top is yellow. B: The girl's top is pink. 3. At the bus stop Part 1: 1 bus stop, 2 raining, 3 umbrella, 4 bag, 5 green, 6 coat, 7 red Model: In this picture I can see a bus stop. It is raining. A man has a black umbrella. A woman has a bag. She is wearing a green coat. The red bus is coming. I don't like the rain because it is cold. Part 3: 1) A: The umbrella is black. B: The umbrella is red. 2) A: The bus is red. B: The bus is blue. 3) A: The woman's coat is green. B: The woman's coat is purple. 4) A: The woman has a yellow bag. B: The woman has no bag. 5) A: There is a puddle. B: There is no puddle. 4. In the classroom Part 1: 1 classroom, 2 teacher, 3 board, 4 two, 5 sitting, 6 desks, 7 books Model: In this picture I can see a classroom. The teacher is pointing at the board. There are two students. They are sitting at their desks. There are books on the desks. I like learning English because I can talk to people. Part 3: 1) A: The board says ABC. B: The board says 123. 2) A: The teacher's top is purple. B: The teacher's top is pink. 3) A: There is a plant. B: There is no plant. 4) A: There is a clock on the wall. B: There is no clock. 5) A: There are three books. B: There is one book.

e1/speaking-listening/docs/community-cen: E1 Days, Times and Prices – Community Centre – Task 4 Listening and Task 2 Talk – Day Plan and Answers Entry 1 Speaking & Listening · PC room – learners on their own PCs for most of the lesson · about 2 hours · present simple only (is / starts / finishes / costs; What time does it start?) Prep: Nothing for learners to print – everything is on their PCs. Print this plan only if you want it on paper. Before the lesson: post the learners’ page link in Teams General, and check the projector sound. Aims: Understand days, times and prices in short messages and conversations (Task 4); ask and answer What day / What time / How much; give a one-minute talk about "My week" and answer two questions (Task 2). Why this shape: One community-centre timetable runs through the whole lesson, so each activity uses the language from the one before: read → ask → listen → information gap → grammar check → talk. Links: Projector: https://atinwix.github.io/esol/e1/speaking-listening/community-centre-days-times-prices-projector-lesson.html · Learners (PC / phone): https://atinwix.github.io/esol/e1/speaking-listening/community-centre-days-times-prices-interactive-practice.html · Audio: https://atinwix.github.io/esol/e1/speaking-listening/audio/community-centre/ · Vote Card: https://atinwix.github.io/esol/all-levels/classroom-tool-vote-card.html?mode=yn · Hangman text: https://atinwix.github.io/esol/e1/speaking-listening/community-centre-hangman-paragraph-read-aloud-text.html Slide numbers are the dots along the top of the projector page (1 = first dot). The teacher script matches the Teacher note on each slide. If you are ahead: learners ask "What time does it finish?" in the information gap, write a third day in their talk, or post their talk in the class Team (General) using Copy my talk. If you are behind: do Scripts C and D only, and cut the volunteer talks. Answers – Kahoot 1. The computer class is on… – Tuesday 2. What time does football start? – 6 o'clock 3. How much is the English club? – It's free 4. What day is the family film? – Saturday 5. How much is a tea in the café? – 80p 6. The sewing class starts at… – half past ten 7. Choose the correct sentence. – The class starts at two. 8. Choose the correct question. – What time does it start? 9. ___ Saturday I go to the family film. – On 10. The film starts ___ three o'clock. – at 11. Script A: Is the yoga class on Wednesday? – Yes, it is. 12. Script B: How much is the music class? – £2 13. Script C: What time is the art class? – half past one 14. Script D: Is the library open on Sunday? – No, it isn't. 15. Script F: How much is the dance class? – It's free 16. £2.50 – how do we say it? – two pounds fifty 17. 50p means… – fifty pence 18. My friend ___ to the cooking class. – goes 19. Which day comes after Tuesday? – Wednesday 20. Is the café open every day? – Yes, it is. Tab 2 Listening: listen twice, answer; then say the answers 1 Yes, it is. 2 Seven o'clock. Script: Ann: Hello. This is Riverside Community Centre. We have a new yoga class. It is on Wednesday. Goodbye. 31–35 Script B on the PC (conversation), checked together (Individual, then whole class) Slide 7 "Script B – on your PC"; learners' page Tab 2 Listening Say: 'Look at Script B on your PC. Read question 1 and question 2.' Read both aloud. Press ▶ Play twice (it plays, pauses, then plays again). Learners choose Yes or No and type answer 2 on their PC (they press Check after Script F, not now). Then check here: ask question 1 and 'How much is the music class?' – take answers from 3–4 learners. Press Show answer three times: answer 1, then answer 2, then the script. Tab 2 Listening: listen twice, answer; read the script 1 No, it isn't. It's on Friday. 2 Two pounds (£2). Script: Ben: Hello. Is there a music class? Ann: Yes, there is. It's on Friday. Ben: What time does it start? Ann: It starts at four o'clock. Ben: How much is it? Ann: It's two pounds. 35–47 Scripts C–F: listen and answer on the PC (Individual) Slide 8 "Scripts C to F – on your PC"; learners' page Tab 2 Listening Say: 'You already have 2 Listening open. Don't stop between scripts to check. When all four are done, say 'Press Check'. Then go through the answers here: press Show answer for each script, then Next. Ask 'Who has the same?' each time. Choose the missing words. Then read the script with your partner. One person is Ann, one person is Ben. Then change.' Walk round; listen to the pronunciation of times and prices. 8 minutes. Press Show answer to check the missing words together. Say: 'Partner A, open the activity and click 3 Partner A. Partner B, click 3 Partner B. Don't look at your partner's screen! You have different information.' Read the example with a strong learner: you are A. Say: 'Ask your partner questions. Type the answers in the white boxes. When you finish, press Check.' Pairs work. 15–20 minutes. Walk round: listen for 'What time does … start?' and 'It's on …'. Fast pairs: tell them to ask 'What time does it finish?' and invent the answer. Then go to the next slide and check together. Keep this copy off the board. Entry 1: Phoning the doctor’s surgery Receptionist: Good morning, Mare Street Surgery. How can I help you? Rosa: Hello. I’d like to make an appointment with a doctor, please. Receptionist: Of course. What is your name? Rosa: My name is Rosa Lopez. Receptionist: Thank you, Rosa. What is the problem? Rosa: I have a bad cough. I cough every night. Receptionist: When did the cough start? Rosa: It started last week, on Monday. Receptionist: OK. Can you come on Thursday at ten o’clock? Rosa: Sorry, I go to college on Thursday morning. Is the afternoon OK? Receptionist: Yes. Is three o’clock OK? Rosa: Yes, three o’clock is fine. Thank you very much. Receptionist: You’re welcome. See you on Thursday. Goodbye. Answers to the examiner’s questions: gist — a woman making a doctor’s appointment; problem — a bad cough; day — Thursday, at three o’clock; why not the morning — she goes to college on Thursday morning. Entry 2: Lena and Sam plan Saturday Lena: Hi Sam, it’s Lena. Are you free on Saturday? Sam: Hi Lena. Yes, I’m free in the afternoon. Why? Lena: I want to go to Broadway Market. Do you want to come with me? Sam: Good idea! I went there last year and the food was amazing. Lena: Yes, the food is the best thing. Shall we meet at the bus stop at two o’clock? Sam: Two o’clock is a bit early for me, because I finish work at half past one. Can we meet at half past two? Lena: OK, half past two. Which bus stop? Sam: The one outside Hackney Central station. Is that OK? Lena: Yes, perfect. But the weather forecast says it might rain on Saturday. Sam: Then let’s bring umbrellas! Or we can go to the cinema instead if it rains a lot. Lena: Good plan. I’ll check the weather again on Saturday morning and text you. Sam: Great. See you on Saturday, Lena! Answers to the examiner’s questions: gist — two friends planning a trip to a market on Saturday; meeting time — half past two (two o’clock is the trap); place — outside Hackney Central station; if it rains a lot — the cinema.

Lesson at a glance Level: E2–E3 (L1 extension). Time: about 2½ hours (whole film first, then clips). Aim: understand short clips; describe places and feelings with adjectives and very / really / absolutely. Film: Voices Past and Present (Child Migrant Stories, 11 min) – youtube.com/watch?v=cjF3FI1ngtY. Use this version – it has English subtitles. (The newer 4K version has none.) Short stories from people who came to East London as children, 1920s to today. Clips: 1 = 4:28–5:14 (first impressions: religions, winter 1964, snow) 2 = 5:14–6:10 (Manuhar – dream and reality) 3 = 8:31–10:05 (what is home? L1 only). Play each twice. People in the film: Henry – El Salvador, 17, 1977 • Marie Lyse – Rwanda, 12, 1994 • Max – Ireland, 12, 1927/28 • Duncan – India, 8, 1956 • Manzila – Bangladesh, 13, 1972 • Manuhar – Bangladesh, early 1970s. Others from Jamaica, Turkey, Poland, Brazil, Somalia. Sensitivity: the opening minutes mention killing and war. Start clips at the times given. Task 6 can be about the first day at college. Stages Differentiation Weaker (E2): Task 5 Part A + Part B 1–3; frame on S14. Stronger (E3): add a reason (because …). L1: extension letter with strong adjectives. Answer key Task 1: 1 c 2 e 3 d 4 f 5 a 6 b Task 2: a A b B c A d A Task 3: a T b F (a very cold winter) c T d F (they were happy – they made five snowmen) Task 4: a A b fantastic, beautiful, colourful c B Task 5A: good – fantastic, beautiful, exciting, colourful, wonderful; bad – cold, dirty, terrible, boring, freezing (accept cold/freezing as good if learners like the cold!) Task 5B: 1 very 2 absolutely 3 absolutely 4 very 5 very 6 absolutely (really is correct in all six) Clip 2 – what Manuhar says (if the video fails) “London was something very exciting, because I read a book called London at Night, and it was very, very fascinating. I first arrived in the airport. It was fantastic. Very nice. It is like heaven. So beautiful. So many lights. It was New Year’s Day. It was colourful everywhere. … But when I came here, to the actual place where I am going to live, I said, ‘Oh my God, this is even worse than some places in Bangladesh.’ I could see the difference between the dream and reality.” Games (buttons on slide 13) Millionaire: https://atinwix.github.io/esol/games/millionaire-quiz.html?set=film-vpp Hangman paragraph: Many children came to London from other countries. Some came because of war, and some came to find work. One person arrived in the winter of 1964. It was very cold, and there were thirteen blankets on the bed! Manuhar from Bangladesh thought London was fantastic. The airport was beautiful and colourful. But his new home was terrible. Today, Henry from El Salvador says that Hackney is his home. https://atinwix.github.io/Hangman-Paragraphs-Game/? Today I can… 1 make comparatives cheaper, more expensive, better 2 compare two things with than A bike is cheaper than a car. 3 say what I prefer and why I prefer the bus because it is cheaper. Comparing two things We use adjective + -er / more + than London is bigger than Hackney. A bike is cheaper than a car. A taxi is more expensive than a bus. comparative = comparing TWO things Short adjectives: add -er cheap → cheaper just add -er fast → faster just add -er nice → nicer ends in -e: add -r big → bigger 1 vowel + 1 consonant: double it busy → busier ends in -y: change to -ier Long adjectives: more + adjective 2 or more syllables → put more before the adjective expensive → more expensive comfortable → more comfortable crowded → more crowded interesting → more interesting Not: expensiver X Not: more cheaper X Irregular: learn these two! good → better bad → worse Not: gooder X Not: badder X Not: more good X Task 1: make the comparative Write the comparative on your worksheet, then choose the group A–D. cheap expensive fast busy comfortable good big easy crowded bad old healthy A + -er / -r / double B y → -ier C more + adjective D irregular Task 2: check your answers 1. cheaper 2. faster 3. more expensive 4. quieter 5. busier 6. healthier 7. more comfortable 8. better 9. worse Price check: market or supermarket? Market Supermarket £1.20 £1.50 £1.00 £0.80 £1.50 £1.10 Bananas (1 kg) Tomatoes (500 g) Bread Which is cheaper? Which is more expensive? Tell your partner. Life is a Destiny What would you save? E2 – E3 • Second conditional Warmer Imagine you must leave your home today. You can take only ONE thing. What would you take? Why? You can talk about a real or an imaginary person. Meet Argun Born: Cyprus, 1949 1963–64: war – his school closed, his family lived in tents 1964: came to London, aged 13, to live with his parents First jobs: a Wimpy burger bar, then clothes, then printing Today: he has a printing shop on Mare Street, Hackney! He took only one thing to London. What do you think it was? Key words possessions burgle (past: burgled) emergency keep in contact stepfather proud endure destiny Task 1 Match the words to the meanings on your worksheet. Work with a partner. Key words – answers 1 possessions – c the things you own 2 burgle – h break into a home and steal things 3 emergency – f a sudden, dangerous situation – you must act fast 4 keep in contact – d talk or write to someone regularly 5 stepfather – a your mother’s new husband 6 proud – g pleased about what someone in your family has done 7 endure – b live through something very difficult 8 destiny – e what will happen in your life – you can’t change it Watch the whole film Task 2 Read the questions first. Watch the whole film. Circle A, B or C. Don’t worry about every word! ▶ Play the whole film Whole film – answers and talk Task 2 a B Cyprus b B because of war c A his photo album d B proud Talk in pairs How did you feel? We will watch it twice. ▶ Play clip 1 Clip 2 (10:15 – 12:02) Task 4 Hurmus – Argun’s wife Alara – his granddaughter Who says it? Write H, A or G (Argun). Why would Alara take her phone? ▶ Play clip 2 Clip 1 and 2 – answers Task 3 a T b F – he hid it c T d F – they lived in tents e T f F – it was still there Task 4 a A (Alara) b H (Hurmus) c G (Argun) d A (Alara) Why the phone? B to keep in contact with her family Grammar: the second conditional Alara: “If my house was being bombed, I would take my phone.” If + past simple, would + verb If I had to leave, I would take my phone. I would take my phone if I had to leave. We use it for imaginary or unlikely situations – now or in the future. When ‘if’ comes first, we use a comma ( , ). Who is she going to meet on Wednesday? her friend Rosa She's going to meet her friend Rosa. What are they going to buy? vegetables They're going to buy vegetables. Is she going to go to the gym? e2/reading/docs/personal-hygiene-at-work: E2 Reading – Personal Hygiene at Work – A Problem at Work Name: ______________________________ Date: ______________ Task 1 – Read the story Tom works in a small shop. He is friendly and hardworking. But Tom has a problem – he doesn’t wash very often. His clothes smell, and his breath is not fresh. Tom also smokes, and his clothes smell of tobacco. One day, Tom’s manager, Sara, decides to talk to him. She is kind but honest. She tells Tom that he needs to shower every day, wash his clothes more often and use deodorant. She also tells him to brush his teeth twice a day. Tom is a little embarrassed, but he says thank you. The next week, he comes to work clean and fresh. His co-workers are happy, and Tom feels more confident too. Where does Tom work? ______________________________________________ What is Tom’s problem? ______________________________________________ Who talks to Tom about it? ______________________________________________ What does Sara tell Tom to do? Write two things. ______________________________________________ How does Tom feel at first? ______________________________________________ How does Tom feel at the end? ______________________________________________ Task 2 – Put the conversation in order Number the lines 1–8. Number 1 has been done for you. _____ Tom: I understand. I’m sorry. I’ll shower every morning. _____ Sara: You need to shower every day and wash your clothes more often. _____ Tom: Thank you, Sara. I will. __1__ Sara: Can I talk to you for a minute, Tom? _____ Sara: I need to tell you something important. It’s about personal hygiene. _____ Tom: Oh… OK. What’s the problem? _____ Sara: Don’t worry. Just try to remember from now on. _____ Tom: Of course, Sara. Is everything OK? Passing Tides Linh’s journey E2 – E3 • Past simple and sequencing Warmer How did you come to college today? First I … Then I … How long did it take? Meet Linh Born: Vietnam, 1972 Her father: a university teacher – the police came to their house Aged 7: left Vietnam on a tiny boat with her father Then: Singapore → a camp in England → Hackney 5 years later: her mum, sister and brother came too Vietnam → Singapore → UK. How did she travel? Key words tiny wade crowded pirates rescue refugee camp Task 1 Match the words to the meanings on your worksheet. Key words – answers 1 tiny – c very, very small 2 wade – d walk through deep water 3 crowded – e full of people 4 pirates – f criminals who attack ships at sea 5 rescue – a save someone from danger 6 refugee camp – b a place where refugees live for a short time Watch the whole film Task 2 Read the questions first. Watch the whole film. Circle A, B or C. Don’t worry about every word! ▶ Play the whole film Whole film – answers and talk Task 2 a B Vietnam b B by boat c C her father d B 5 years Talk in pairs How did you feel? What surprised you? What would you ask Linh? Clip 1 (2:54 – 5:11) Task 3 Read the sentences first. Watch. Circle True or False. We will watch it twice. ▶ Play clip 1 Clip 2 (5:11 – 6:56) Task 4 What happened next? Put the events in order: 1 – 5. ▶ Play clip 2 Clip 1 and 2 – answers Task 3 a F – her father b T c T d F – about fifty e F – no food f T Task 4 1 stayed next to the ship 2 women and children on 3 men on 4 camp in Singapore 5 to Britain Grammar: past simple Regular: wait → waited stay → stayed rescue → rescued Irregular: leave → left get → got find → found throw → threw go → went have → had Negative: They didn’t have any food. (not ✗ didn’t had) Linh left Vietnam when she was seven. Telling a story First, they waited in the water. Then they got on a tiny boat. After that, a British ship found them. Finally, they went to Britain. Question: Where did you go? How did you travel? What happened next? Lesson at a glance Level: E2–E3 (L1 extension). Time: about 2½ hours (whole film first, then clips). Aim: follow a story in two clips; tell a story in the past simple with First / Then / After that / Finally. Film: Passing Tides (Child Migrant Stories, 18 min) – youtube.com/watch?v=3ePfMggJoFc. Linh left Vietnam by boat with her father when she was seven (1979). A British ship rescued them. They lived in camps in Singapore and on Thorney Island, then in Hackney. Clips: 1 = 2:54–5:11 (the sea escape) 2 = 5:11–6:56 (the British ship, Singapore) 3 = 6:56–10:49 (life in England, L1 only). Subtitles on. Play each twice. Sensitivity: the film is about a dangerous sea journey. Some learners may have made similar journeys. In Tasks 6 and 7 any journey is fine – to college this morning is a good model. Never ask learners about their journey to the UK in front of the class. Stages Differentiation Weaker (E2): Task 5 verb table + gaps 1–5; use sentence starters. Stronger (E3): add a time phrase in each sentence (in 2019, two days later …). L1: extension. Answer key Task 1: 1 c 2 d 3 e 4 f 5 a 6 b Task 2: a B b B c C d B Task 3: a F (with her father) b T c T d F (about fifty) e F (they ran out of food) f T Task 4: Singapore 4 men on ship 3 stayed next to ship 1 to Britain 5 women and children 2 Task 5 verbs: waited, stayed, rescued, arrived, left, got, found, threw, went, had, saw, took Task 5 story: 1 left 2 waited 3 got 4 didn’t have 5 found 6 threw 7 stayed 8 went Clip 1 – what Linh says (shortened, if the video fails) “My family tried to escape a few times, but there was only enough money for two tickets, for my dad and one other. I was very frightened because we had to wade in the water, with just my head above the water, waiting to board. There were about fifty of us in this tiny boat. The boat was rocking and filling up with water … Suddenly there was this enormous British ship. We had run out of food a couple of days before. They threw down some food – cream crackers and green apples.” Games (buttons on slide 13) Millionaire: https://atinwix.github.io/esol/games/millionaire-quiz.html?set=film-pt Hangman paragraph: Linh was born in Vietnam. When she was seven, she left Vietnam with her father. First, they waited in the water. Then they got on a tiny boat with about fifty people. After a few days, they had no food. Then a big British ship found them. The sailors threw down crackers and green apples. After that, they stayed in a camp in Singapore. Finally, they went to Britain and lived in Hackney. https://atinwix.github.io/Hangman-Paragraphs-Game/? B: Yesterday I went to the shop and I bought some bread and some eggs. C: Yesterday I went to the shop and I bought some bread, some eggs and … Next round: “Last weekend I saw …” / “Last night I ate …” Worksheet 3: was / were Part A: Write was, were, wasn’t or weren’t The bus __________ very busy this morning. My children __________ at school yesterday. I __________ at college on Monday. I was ill. __________ you at home last night? The shops __________ open on Sunday evening. They were closed. The weather __________ nice on Saturday. It was sunny. Part B: How was it? Match the question and the answer. 1 ____ 2 ____ 3 ____ 4 ____ Part C: Ask your partner Ask “How was …?” Answer: It was + word + because … great · good · OK · boring · busy · quiet · tiring · terrible How was your weekend? How was your journey to college today? How was your last birthday? Worksheet 4: Questions and “didn’t” (Task 1) Remember: after did and didn’t, the verb is not in the past. Did you went to the market? ____________________________ I didn’t see my friend yesterday. ____________________________ Where you went on Saturday? ____________________________ She goed to Dalston by bus. ____________________________ What did you ate for lunch? ____________________________ We didn’t went to college on Friday. ____________________________ Did you like the film? ____________________________ I was go to the park last week. ____________________________ Part C: Find someone who … Walk around the class. Ask “Did you …?” Then ask one more question. Answer + one more thing: “Yes, I did. I went to Ridley Road. It was very busy.” Worksheet 5: When? and In what order? Part A: Write last, ago, in or yesterday I came to London two years __________. I went to the doctor __________ week. My son was born __________ 2019. I saw my friend __________ afternoon. We moved to Hackney three months __________. I didn’t go to college __________ Friday. Part B: Put the story in order Nour’s day out. Number the sentences 1–6. Part C: Your turn Tell your partner about yesterday. Use all the words. First … Then … After that … In the evening … Finally … Worksheet 6: My talk about the past (Task 2) Part A: Read Tomasz’s talk Underline the past verbs. Circle First, Then, After that, Finally. “I want to tell you about my last birthday. It was in June. In the morning I went to college as normal, and my classmates sang Happy Birthday. I was very surprised! After college I met my brother in Hackney Central. First, we went to a Turkish restaurant on Mare Street. I had chicken and rice and my brother had a kebab. Then we walked to London Fields. It was warm, so we sat on the grass and talked for a long time. After that, my brother gave me a present. It was a new watch. Finally, I phoned my mum in Poland. She was happy, and I felt happy too. It was a really good day.” How many past verbs did you find? ______ Where did Tomasz eat? ______________________________ What was his present? ______________________________ How did he feel at the end? ______________________________ Part B: Make it longer Add who, where, why or how you felt. I went to the park. → I went to the park with my children because it was sunny. I cooked dinner. → ____________________________________________ I watched a film. → ____________________________________________ I went shopping. → ____________________________________________ Part C: Plan your talk Choose a topic. You have one minute. Write words, not sentences. What you did last weekend A special day or celebration (a wedding, Eid, Christmas, a birthday) A day out in London Your first day at this college A meal you cooked for other people Part D: Listen to your partner Tick when you hear it. ☐ past verbs (went, had, saw …) ☐ First / Then / After that / Finally ☐ a feeling (happy, tired, surprised …) ☐ talks for about two minutes Then ask two questions: What did you …? Who did you …? Did you …? Why did you …? How was …? Rule Example Most verbs: + ed walk → walked Verb ends in e: + d live → lived Consonant + y: y → ied study → studied Short verb, vowel + consonant: double it stop → stopped t (walked) d (played) id (wanted) Verb Past Verb Past go went see __________ have __________ meet __________ eat __________ make __________ buy bought get __________ take __________ come __________ do __________ feel felt sleep __________ leave __________ say __________ give __________ drink __________ find __________ speak spoke write __________ Yes No Question I / he / she / it was wasn’t Was it …? you / we / they were weren’t Were you …? e2/speaking-listening/docs/esb-exam-prep: E2 Speaking and Listening Exam Prep - Lesson Plan and Answers - Version 1 Oct 7, 2026 · @Atin Exam at a glance Learners take the exam in pairs. It has four tasks and about 25 minutes of guide time. This follows ESB Entry 2 sample Set O; check your live ESB set for any changes. The last column is from the ESB Assessors’ Report 2023-24. The report names note-making in the thinking minute at Entry 1; confirm with ESB that notes are allowed at Entry 2 before you promise it to learners. Lesson overview One 120-minute lesson that walks learners through all four tasks, with most practice time on the points assessors flag. If you need a 10-minute break, take it after Stage 3 and cut Stage 6 to a two-minute recap. By the end, learners can: say what happens in each of the four tasks ask at least six correct personal questions and one follow-up question give a talk of one to two minutes about a past event from key-word notes compare two pictures using comparatives and say which they prefer answer a yes/no gist question and a detail question on a short spoken text You need: the Student Handouts document (one copy each), two pairs of photos to project, a timer, scrap paper. No audio is needed: you read the listening texts aloud. Stage-by-stage plan Stage 1: What happens in the exam? (0-10) Learners leave this stage able to say what each task is. Board: ESB Speaking and Listening exam. Ask: “Who is in the room?” (you, a partner, the assessor). “How long is it?” (about 25 minutes). “Do you write?” (no). Handout 1, Part A. Learners match the four tasks to what you do. Three minutes alone, then compare with a partner. Part B, true or false. Check as a class and correct the false sentences aloud. Say: “The assessor wants to hear you talk. Do not learn a speech. Listen to the question and answer it.” Stage 2: Asking and answering questions - Task 1 (10-35) The target is correct question forms in three times, plus real follow-up questions instead of a memorised list. Board (2 min). Write NOW / LAST WEEK / NEXT YEAR. Elicit one question under each: What do you do…? What did you do…? What are you going to do…? Underline do / did / are. Handout 2, Part A (8 min). Learners build eight questions from prompts. Check on the board. Drill chorally, then individually: falling voice at the end of Wh- questions, and “did you” said as one sound. Follow-up questions (5 min). Model with a confident learner. You: “Where do you live?” Learner: “In Hackney.” You: “Do you like it? … Why?” Point to Part B on the handout: Why? / Do you like it? / How often? / Who with? / What is it like? Question chain (8 min). Pairs. A asks a question from Part A. B answers with a full sentence and one more thing. A must then ask one follow-up question that is not on the page. Swap. Change partners after four minutes. Feedback (2 min). Board three question errors you heard, without names. Learners correct them. Board the rule: Answer + one more thing. “I live in Hackney. It is busy but I like it.” Accept “I live in a hotel in…” and “I’d like to be a…” as full answers. Do not push for details on family, country or the journey here. Stage 3: The two-minute talk - Task 2 (35-60) The target is a talk about a past event, built from key-word notes made in one minute. Listen (3 min). Handouts face down. Read Amina’s talk aloud (the full text is in the answers below). Ask: “Did she have a good day?” (Yes.) “Where did she go?” (Victoria Park.) Handout 3, Part A (7 min). Learners complete the talk with past simple verbs. Check. Drill went, took, saw, made, bought, felt. Notes, not sentences (3 min). Show Amina’s notes in Part B. Ask: “Are these sentences?” (No, words.) “How long to write them?” (One minute.) Thinking minute (2 min). Each learner picks a topic from Part C. Time one minute of silent note-making in the box. Stop them at 60 seconds. Talk, round 1 (4 min). Pairs. A talks for 90 seconds. B listens, then asks two questions using the starters in Part D. Swap. Talk, round 2 (4 min). New partner, same topic, full two minutes each if time allows, otherwise 90 seconds. The second attempt is always longer and more accurate; tell them so. Feedback (2 min). Board two good sentences you heard and two past-tense errors to correct. If a speaker stops early, the partner says “And then?” or “Tell me more.” Teach both phrases before round 1. Stage 4: Describe and compare pictures - Task 3 (60-85) The target is three steps every time: describe, compare, opinion. Comparatives are the weak point at this level. Project two photos side by side. Suggested pairs: Pair A: a street market (Ridley Road Market) and a supermarket Pair B: a park (London Fields) and a busy shopping street Pair C (spare): a bus and a bicycle Vocabulary (5 min). Show Pair A. Elicit what learners can see into two board columns, one per picture. Model: “There is a… / There are some… / The people are buying…” Handout 4, Parts A and B (8 min). Learners complete the comparatives table, then the five sentences. Check. Board the rule: short word + er (cheaper); y changes to ier (busier); long word = more (more expensive); good becomes better. Model the three steps (3 min). Speak for one minute about Pair A yourself. Learners tick the steps in Part C as they hear them: 1 Describe. 2 Compare (“Both pictures show… but…”). 3 Opinion (“I prefer… because…”). Pairs (7 min). Show Pair B. A speaks for two minutes using the three steps. B ticks the steps, then asks: “Which do you prefer? Why?” Swap, using Pair A or Pair C. Feedback (2 min). Correct one comparative error on the board. Praise anyone who said what is the same as well as what is different. Stage 5: Listening and discussion - Task 4 (85-110) The target is hearing the topic first, then one detail. You read both texts aloud. Explain (2 min). “You hear two texts. You hear each one two times. First time: I ask yes or no. Second time: I ask a question first, then you listen for the answer. In the exam you say the answer. Today you write it, so everyone can practise.” Text 1 (8 min). Read at natural speed. Turn your head or change voice for the two speakers. Learners tick yes or no for questions 1 and 2 on Handout 5. Read questions 3 and 4 aloud, then read the text again. Learners write short answers. Check. Text 2 (7 min). Same steps. Discussion (6 min). Groups of three: two learners and one “assessor” who asks the questions in Part C. Three minutes, then change the assessor. Point to the useful phrases first. Feedback (2 min). Ask two groups what their partner said. Text 1 - at the library Librarian: Good afternoon. Can I help you? Customer: Yes, please. I want to join the library. How much does it cost? Librarian: It’s free. Do you have a letter with your name and address? Customer: No, I left it at home. I only have my college card. Librarian: That’s OK. Bring the letter tomorrow and I can make your card then. Customer: Thank you. What time do you close tomorrow? Librarian: We close at six o’clock. The computers are on the first floor, next to the children’s books. Customer: Great. See you tomorrow. Text 2 - the community garden Good morning everyone. I want to tell you about the new community garden near the college. It opens on Monday. First, there is a vegetable garden. You can grow tomatoes and potatoes there, and you can take them home. Next to the gate there is a small kitchen where you can make tea and coffee. Every Wednesday afternoon there is a free gardening class. It starts at two o’clock and you don’t need to book. Please wear old shoes because the garden is often wet. I hope you enjoy the garden and come often. Stage 6: Mini mock and self-check (110-120) Learners run a six-minute version of the exam, then mark their own confidence. Mini mock (6 min). Pairs, using the card on Handout 6. One minute each asking questions. One minute each talking about yesterday. One minute each on a picture pair left on the board. Time it aloud. Self-check (3 min). Learners tick the “I can” list on Handout 6. Collect a show of hands for the hardest task; that is your next lesson. Homework (1 min). Choose one topic from Handout 3, Part C. Make notes for one minute. Talk for two minutes with a phone timer. Answers Handout 1 Part A: 1 c, 2 d, 3 a, 4 b. Part B: 1 False (with a partner). 2 True. 3 False (two minutes). 4 True. 5 True. 6 False (you say your answers). Handout 2 Where do you live? Who do you live with? What do you do at the weekend? Are there any shops near your home? What did you do last weekend? What did you eat yesterday? What are you going to do next year? What job would you like in the future? Handout 3 Part A: 1 went, 2 took, 3 was, 4 walked, 5 saw, 6 had, 7 made, 8 bought, 9 rained, 10 went, 11 felt. Full text to read aloud: Last Saturday I went to Victoria Park with my friend Sara. We took the bus because it was a long walk. First, we walked around the lake and we saw a lot of ducks. Then we had a picnic. I made rice and chicken, and Sara bought some fruit from the market. In the afternoon it rained, so we went home early. I felt tired but happy. It was a good day. Handout 4 Part A: bigger, cheaper, quieter, busier, noisier, more expensive, more crowded, better. Part B: 1 busier, 2 quieter, 3 cheaper, 4 more expensive, 5 better. Handout 5 Task What learners do Guide time What to work on (assessors’ report) 1 Exchange of personal information Ask each other questions, then answer the assessor’s questions on area, work or study, plans and events 5 min Answers sound memorised; question forms get weaker later in the exam 2 Unprepared talk Talk for 2 minutes on a topic from the assessor, usually a past event. Partner listens and asks two questions 6 min Use the one-minute preparation time; practise the long turn 3 Describing pictures Describe two pictures, compare them and give an opinion, for about 2 minutes 4 min Comparatives; saying what is the same and what is different 4 Listening and discussion Hear two short texts, each played twice. A yes/no gist question, then a detail question. Then a 3-minute discussion on the topic 10 min Listening for gist Time Stage Exam task Handout 0-10 1 What happens in the exam? All 1 10-35 2 Asking and answering questions Task 1 2 35-60 3 The two-minute talk Task 2 3 60-85 4 Describe and compare pictures Task 3 4 85-110 5 Listening and discussion Task 4 5 110-120 6 Mini mock and self-check All 6 Text Question Answer 1 Library 1 Is this about buying books? No 1 Library 2 Is this about joining a library? Yes 1 Library 3 How much does it cost to join the library? It is free / nothing 1 Library 4 What time does the library close tomorrow? (At) six o’clock 2 Garden 1 Is this about a new garden? Yes 2 Garden 2 Is this about a cooking class? No 2 Garden 3 When does the garden open? (On) Monday 2 Garden 4 What time does the gardening class start? (At) two o’clock

e3/reading/describing-hackney-adjectives: E3 Reading – Describing Hackney – Adjectives and Adverbs – Projector Lesson E3 Reading · Adjectives and adverbs · PC room Describing Hackney Adjective or adverb? Find the mistakes on your PC, check your place on the map, then write about your favourite place. Do: PCs logged in. Find the error link posted in Teams General. Say: “This afternoon: adjectives and adverbs. Then you will check your place on the map and write about your favourite place in London.” Adjective or adverb? What does the word describe? Adjective → a thing or a place a busy market The water is warm . After be : is, was, are … Adverb → how we do it Traders shout loudly . Ride slowly . After the action: shout, ride, walk … quick → quick ly careful → careful ly happy → happ ily easy → eas ily good → well fast → fast hard → hard Do: Point to the two boxes, then the words at the bottom. Say: “This morning we read: ‘Traders shout loudly.’ Shout – HOW? Loudly. That’s an adverb. ‘A busy market’ – busy describes the market. That’s an adjective. … Careful: good becomes WELL. Fast stays fast. Hard stays hard. … A quiet street or a quietly street? Speak quiet or speak quietly?” Adjective or adverb? · Come to the board Choose the right word Do: Learners come to the board one at a time and click. Say: “Come to the board. Choose the right word. Class – is it describing a thing, or HOW someone does it? … Careful with the last one: hardly does NOT mean hard!” PCs · On your own Find the error Open Find the error from the Teams post (or scan the code with your phone). Tap the word that is wrong. Type the correct sentence. 20 sentences. Finished? Search for your place from this morning. Find the nearest station, the opening times, and how long it takes to walk there from college. Read the reviews – find two adjectives. … Ridley Road group – what is the nearest station?” PCs · Write and post Write about your favourite place My favourite place is Victoria Park. It is a large , green park near Hackney Wick. In the morning it is very quiet . I walk slowly round the lake and watch the ducks. There is a lovely café, and the coffee is cheap . Write 4–5 sentences about a place you like in London. Use three adjectives and one adverb . Post it in Teams → General . Start with the name of the place. Do: Read the example aloud. Point out the highlighted adjectives and the underlined adverb. Say: “Now write about YOUR favourite place in London. Four or five sentences. Three adjectives and one adverb – like my example. Post it in Teams, General. Start with the name of the place.” PCs · Read and reply Read two posts and reply Read two classmates’ posts. Reply to each one with one question . Answer the questions people ask you. Is it expensive? How do you get there? When is it open? Who do you go with? Is it busy at the weekend? Do: When most have replied, put two posts on the screen: praise good adjectives and correct one mistake together. Say: “Read two of your classmates’ posts. Reply to each one with ONE question. Then answer the questions people ask you.” Game · Whole class Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? Teacher: open the game on the projector – today’s questions are already loaded. Everyone faces the screen. Read each question aloud. The whole class votes A, B, C or D (hands up). The teacher clicks the class’s answer. Vote card Scan, then hold up A, B, C or D Open the game – questions are loaded ▶ 15 questions on today’s adjectives, adverbs and places. Do: Everyone away from the PCs, facing the screen. Learners open the Vote card on their phones (QR top right). Click the button – the questions are already loaded. You run it. Say: “Let’s play Who Wants to Be a Millionaire! I read the question. Everyone holds up your vote card – A, B, C or D. … Most people say B – final answer? OK!” Before you go · Pairs Quiet or quietly? Say one sentence with quiet and one with quietly . Say one sentence with good and one with well . Tell your partner: “Next time I read a new word, I will …” Do: Pairs, 3 minutes. Say: “Before you go: make one sentence with quiet and one with quietly. One with good and one with well. … Thank you, everyone. See you on Wednesday!” 🗣 Teacher script (T) ‹ ›
e3/reading/hackney-places-adjectives-jig: E3 Reading – Hackney Places – Adjectives and Jigsaw Reading – Projector Lesson E3 Reading · Adjectives · Reading for detail Hackney places Today: read about a place in Hackney, become the expert, and tell your new group about it. Then: what does the word mean? Use the sentence to help you. Do: Do the register. Texts A–D and the question sheets ready on your desk. Say: “Good morning! Today we’re reading about four places in Hackney. You will become an expert on one place – and then teach your group about it.” Settle in · Hangman Paragraphs Guess the paragraph It’s about a place in Hackney. Guess the words one at a time. Work together! Start the game ▶ 📋 Copy text for NaturalReader Do: Click 📋 Copy text for NaturalReader (nothing shows on screen), paste into NaturalReader and play it TWICE – or read it aloud yourself. Then click Start the game. Stuck halfway? Play it once more. Say: “Listen carefully – I’ll read a paragraph twice. Then guess the words! … … Well done. Which words describe the park? (large, green, quiet, busy) Which words tell us HOW people do things? (slowly, happily) – Write both lists on the board and keep them for this afternoon.” Lead-in · Pairs Do you know these places? 🍉 Ridley Road Market 🏊 London Fields and the Lido 🥐 Broadway Market 🦆 The Regent’s Canal Have you been to any of these places? When? Who with? What can you do or buy there? Is there a place like this near where you live? Do: Pairs, 2 minutes. Then take ideas and write them on the board. Say: “Look at these four places. Talk to your partner: have you been there? What can you do or buy there? … Who has been to Ridley Road? What did you buy?” Words to describe places · Whole class Match the word and the meaning Tap a word, then tap its meaning. Do: Learners come to the board one at a time. Then drill and pair test. Say: “These words describe places. Come and match the word and the meaning. … Repeat after me: COLourful. exPENsive. FAmous. … Now pairs: A says the meaning, B says the word.” Predict · Pairs Which place do you think is…? Guess with your partner. Don’t read yet! Click to check after the reading. busy and noisy → Ridley Road Market calm and quiet → The Regent’s Canal expensive → Broadway Market open all year, even in December → London Fields Lido good for families with children → London Fields full of people at the weekend → Broadway Market Do: Pairs guess. Do NOT click yet – you come back here after slide 8. Say: “Don’t read anything yet! Guess with your partner: which place is busy and noisy? Which is calm and quiet? … We’ll check after the reading.” Activity 1 · Expert groups Read and become the expert Sit in your group: A, B, C or D . Each group has a different place. Read your text alone . Answer the questions for your place only : A 1–5 · B 6–10 · C 11–15 · D 16–20. Underline the words that prove each answer. Write the question number next to them. Check with your group. Everyone must agree – and be able to prove it. Start 15 min Pause Reset Do: Give each table its own text (A, B, C or D) and everyone a question sheet. Click Start 15 min. Walk round and check every group’s answers and underlining (day plan, Answers) – experts must be right before they move. Fast finishers: read the other places’ questions so they know what to ask. Say: “Your table has one place. Read it alone first – no talking. Answer only the questions for your place: A is 1 to 5, B is 6 to 10, C is 11 to 15, D is 16 to 20. Underline the words that prove each answer and write the question number next to them. Then check with your group. You are the experts – you will teach the others!” Activity 2 · New groups Teach your group – and prove it New groups: one A, one B, one C and one D. Take your text and your question sheet. Expert: give the answers for your place. Prove each one – read your underlined words aloud. Don’t show the text. Everyone else: write the answer and the paragraph. Ask questions! Question 6 is D, because paragraph 1 says … Which paragraph? Can you read it again? How do you know? Start 20 min Pause Reset Do: Make new groups: one A, one B, one C, one D at each table (one group has two As). Click Start 20 min – about 4–5 minutes per expert. Listen for experts who only say the letter: make them read the proof. Say: “Now change tables. Each new group needs an A, a B, a C and a D. Take your text and your question sheet – but don’t show your text. Experts: give your answers and prove them – read the words you underlined. Everyone else: write the answer and the paragraph number. If they don’t say the paragraph, ask: ‘Which paragraph?’” Activity 2 · Check together Check all 20 answers Someone who wasn’t the expert gives the answer. The expert proves it. Then click. Show all 🍉 Ridley Road Market 1 Dalston Kingsland · para 1 2 B – things to cook food from home · para 2 3 C – late in the day · para 3 4 A – some stalls don’t take cards · para 4 5 any two: fruit, vegetables, fish, meat, fabrics, kitchen things · para 2 🏊 London Fields and the Lido 6 D – a meal on the grass · para 1 7 A – the water is made warm · para 2 8 B – False (“not free”) · para 2 9 C – reserve a place online · para 2 10 any two: football, table tennis, swimming · para 1–2 🥐 Broadway Market 11 A – calm, a few small shops · para 1 12 Saturday and Sunday · para 1 13 D – tasty but costs a lot · para 2 14 C – check all the prices first · para 2 15 any two: bread, cheese, cakes, flowers, hot food · para 2 🦆 The Regent’s Canal 16 B – walk or cycle · para 1 17 D – some homes are on the canal · para 2 18 C – slowly, ring the bell · para 3 19 A – unhealthy for them · para 3 20 any two: ducks, swans, a heron · para 2 Do: Go 1 to 20. Ask a learner who was NOT the expert for that place for the answer, then ask an expert for the proof (read the underlined words). Then click the box. If many got it wrong, ask the expert to read the line again. After 20, press ← three times to slide 5 and check the predictions. Say: “Let’s check all twenty. Question 1 – not the Ridley Road experts – what’s the answer? … Ridley Road expert: prove it! Which paragraph? Read it to us.” Activity 3 · Word meaning in context What does the word mean? Read the sentence. Try each answer in place of the word. Which one makes sense? Vote card Scan, then hold up A, B, C or D Do: Phones out: learners scan the Vote card QR (top right). Read the sentence. Ready? Hold up your answer – A, B, C or D! … What is the clue in the sentence? … Try the answer in place of the word. Does it make sense?” Activity 3 · Word meaning in context What does the word mean? In the exam: read the sentence before and after. The text gives you the clue. Vote card Scan, then hold up A, B, C or D Do: Same as the last slide. Say: “Remember: no dictionary in the exam. Read the sentence before and after the word – the text gives you the clue. Vote cards up: A, B, C or D?” Kahoot! Hackney places quiz Go to kahoot.it on your phone and enter the game PIN. 20 questions: words from the texts, details about the four places, adjective or adverb? Two or three learners share with the class. Say: “Tell your partner about a place near where you live. Where is it? What can you do there? Use two adjectives. … Thank you! e3/reading/docs/hackney-places-adjective: E3 Reading – Hackney Places – Adjectives, Adverbs and Jigsaw Reading – Day Plan and Answers Two lessons on one topic: four Hackney places. Morning: adjectives for places and a jigsaw reading (read for detail, share information, work out word meaning from context). Afternoon, PC room: adjectives and adverbs, an online error hunt, a maps task, and writing a short description for Teams. Aims: Learners can find specific details in a short descriptive text; explain the meaning of a word from the sentence around it; choose between an adjective and an adverb; describe a familiar place with three adjectives. Exam skills: Reading for detail when the question uses different words from the text; word meaning in context; proving an answer from one sentence. Prep: Before the morning: arrange the room as four tables (A, B, C, D) and check the Kahoot opens (link on slide 11). Before 12:30: log the PCs in and post the Find the error link in Teams General. No cutting out. Print: One file, print once, double-sided (43 sheets): your teacher script, then expert texts A ×6, B ×5, C ×5, D ×5 (each on its own sheet), then 21 question sheets (one sheet, both sides). Nothing for the afternoon. Checking learning: Before regrouping, check every expert group’s answers and underlining at the table – the experts must be accurate. In the whole-class check, a learner who was not the expert gives each answer and the expert proves it from their underlining: this shows whether the information was passed on correctly. In the afternoon, Find the error scores show who needs help with adverbs; pick out errors from the Teams posts for whole-class correction. Morning – Hackney places: jigsaw reading (about 9:40–11:45) Afternoon, PC room – Describing Hackney: adjectives and adverbs (about 12:30–2:30) Differentiation: Give weaker readers text B or D and seat two of them in the same expert group; in the jigsaw they may read their underlined words straight from the text. Stronger learners read the other places’ questions in Activity 1 so they are ready to ask, and in the afternoon write 6–8 sentences with two adverbs and reply to three posts. If the morning runs late, shorten Activity 3 (do slide 9 only), not the jigsaw. Answers Slide 4: busy – with a lot of people and activity; noisy – with a lot of loud sound; quiet – with very little sound; colourful – with many bright colours; cheap – does not cost much; expensive – costs a lot; fresh – new, not old (food); large – big; famous – many people know it; polite – nice and kind to other people; lovely – very nice; old – not new; here for a long time. Slide 5 (predictions): busy and noisy – Ridley Road Market; calm and quiet – the Regent’s Canal; expensive – Broadway Market; open all year – London Fields Lido; good for families with children – London Fields; full of people at the weekend – Broadway Market. Text A – Ridley Road Market (questions 1–5): 1 Dalston Kingsland (station) (para 1); 2 B (para 2: “a good place to find ingredients from home”); 3 C (para 3: “especially at the end of the day”); 4 A (para 4: “some small stalls do not take cards”); 5 any two: fruit, vegetables, fish, meat, fabrics, things for the kitchen, food from Africa / the Caribbean / Turkey (para 2). Text B – London Fields and the Lido (questions 6–10): 6 D (para 1: “Families have picnics on the grass”); 7 A (para 2: “the water is heated, so people swim there all year”); 8 B False (para 2: “The lido is not free”); 9 C (para 2: “on busy days it is a good idea to book online”); 10 any two: football, table tennis, swimming (paras 1–2). Text C – Broadway Market (questions 11–15): 11 A (para 1: “During the week it is a quiet street with small shops”); 12 Saturday and Sunday (para 1); 13 D (para 2: “The food is delicious, but it is often expensive”); 14 C (para 2: “look at all the prices before you buy”); 15 any two: bread, cheese, cakes, flowers, hot food, coffee (para 2). Text D – The Regent’s Canal (questions 16–20): 16 B (para 1: “where you can walk or ride a bike”); 17 D (para 2: “Some people live on these boats all year”); 18 C (para 3: “Cyclists should ride slowly and ring their bell”); 19 A (para 3: “it is bad for them”); 20 any two: ducks, swans, a heron (para 2). Slides 9–10 (word meaning): slippery – easy to fall on; traders – people who sell things; heated – made warm; book – reserve a place; crowded – full of people; delicious – very tasty; peaceful – calm and quiet; narrow – not wide. PM slide 3: 1 busy; 2 loudly; 3 carefully; 4 happily; 5 warm; 6 well; 7 good; 8 fast; 9 quiet; 10 slowly; 11 patiently; 12 hard. Find the error: 1 loudly; 2 happily; 3 carefully; 4 well; 5 good; 6 slow; 7 noisy; 8 patiently; 9 peaceful; 10 fast; 11 hard; 12 warm; 13 quietly; 14 correctly; 15 slowly; 16 delicious; 17 clearly; 18 crowded; 19 beautifully; 20 fresh. The page marks itself. Kahoot: 1 noisy; 2 not wide; 3 very tasty; 4 easy to fall on; 5 calm and quiet; 6 made warm; 7 reserve a place; 8 Dalston; 9 end of the day; 10 Some stalls don't take cards; 11 The water is heated; 12 Sat & Sun; 13 11 o'clock; 14 Ride slowly and ring their bell; 15 quickly; 16 well; 17 good; 18 loudly; 19 busy; 20 hard. Millionaire (loads from PM slide 8): 1 Which word is an adjective? – noisy; 2 Which word is an adverb? – carefully; 3 The opposite of 'cheap' is… – expensive; 4 The opposite of 'noisy' is… – quiet; 5 'Please walk ___.' – carefully; 6 'The canal is very ___ in the morning.' – peaceful; 7 The adverb from 'happy' is… – happily; 8 The adverb from 'good' is… – well; 9 'My son runs very ___.' – fast; 10 A place full of people is… – crowded; 11 Narrowboats are… – long and thin; 12 London Fields Lido is… – an outdoor pool; 13 Ridley Road Market is near… – Dalston Kingsland station; 14 At Broadway Market, a coffee and a cake can cost… – £8 or £9; 15 Which sentence is correct? – She sings beautifully.. Links Print everything – class of 21 (print once, double-sided): https://atinwix.github.io/esol/e3/reading/docs/hackney-places-print-all-double-sided-class-of-21.pdf Teacher script (for you): https://atinwix.github.io/esol/e3/reading/docs/hackney-places-teacher-script.pdf AM projector lesson: https://atinwix.github.io/esol/e3/reading/hackney-places-adjectives-jigsaw-reading-projector-lesson.html Kahoot (ready to play): https://create.kahoot.it/share/hackney-adverbs/49b15cf9-dd40-4151-8b4b-d75d05d5d4f2 Kahoot import file (for other teachers): https://atinwix.github.io/esol/e3/reading/docs/hackney-places-adjectives-adverbs-kahoot.xlsx Hangman Paragraphs (paragraph loaded): https://atinwix.github.io/Hangman-Paragraphs-Game/? PM projector lesson: https://atinwix.github.io/esol/e3/reading/describing-hackney-adjectives-adverbs-projector-lesson.html Find the error (PCs and phones): https://atinwix.github.io/esol/e3/reading/adjectives-adverbs-find-the-error-interactive-practice.html Vote card (A–D on phones): https://atinwix.github.io/esol/all-levels/classroom-tool-vote-card.html Millionaire game (questions loaded): https://atinwix.github.io/esol/games/millionaire-quiz.html?set=e3-hackney Time Activity Resources 9:40 (10) Hangman Paragraphs: press the play button in the game to read the paragraph aloud, then click Start the game on slide 2. Read again if they get stuck. When it is solved, ask which words describe the park (large, green, quiet, busy) and which words tell you how people do things (slowly, happily). Leave both lists on the board for the afternoon. Paragraph (teacher only, don't project): Victoria Park is a large, green park in east London. Many people think it is in Hackney, but it is really in Tower Hamlets. In the morning it is quiet and peaceful. People walk slowly round the lake and watch the ducks. At the weekend it is very busy. Children play happily in the playground, and families have picnics on the grass. There is a lovely café by the water, where the coffee is good and the cakes are delicious. In summer, people sit quietly in the sun and read. Don't project this text. AM slide 2 · Hangman Paragraphs 9:50 (10) Lead-in: the four places. Pairs discuss the three questions. Take feedback and board what learners already know about each place. Slide 3 10:00 (15) Words to describe places: learners come to the board in turn to match 12 adjectives to meanings. Drill the stress (COLourful, exPENsive, FAmous). Pairs test each other: one says the meaning, the other says the word. Slide 4 10:15 (5) Predict: pairs guess which place is busy and noisy, calm and quiet, and so on. Don’t reveal – you come back to it after the reading. Slide 5 10:20 (20) Activity 1, expert groups. Each table reads a different text alone (5 min) and answers only its own section of the question sheet (A 1–5, B 6–10, C 11–15, D 16–20). Learners underline the words that prove each answer and write the question number next to them, then check in the group – everyone must agree and be able to prove it. Check every group’s answers and underlining now. Fast finishers read the other places’ questions so they know what to ask. Slide 6 (15-min timer) · Expert texts A–D · Question sheet 10:40 (25) Activity 2, jigsaw. Regroup so each new group has an A, B, C and D; learners take their text and question sheet. Each expert gives the answers for their place (4–5 min) and proves each one by reading their underlined words aloud, without showing the text; the others write the answer and the paragraph and ask questions. Then check all 20 as a class: a learner who was not the expert gives the answer, the expert proves it, then click. Go back to slide 5 and check the predictions. Slides 7 (20-min timer), 8, 5 · Question sheet 11:05 (15) Activity 3, word meaning in context: eight exam-style questions from all four texts. Learners scan the Vote card QR on the slide and hold up A–D on their phones before you click. Each time, ask for the clue in the sentence, and model trying each answer in place of the word. Slides 9–10 11:20 (15) Kahoot, 20 questions: vocabulary, details from the four places, adjective or adverb. Go over the two most-missed questions. Slide 11 · Kahoot file 11:35 (10) Before you go: pairs describe a place near where they live – where, what you can do, two adjectives. Two or three learners share with the class. Slide 12 Time Activity Resources 12:30 (15) Adjective or adverb? Elicit the “how” words from the morning texts (shout loudly, play happily, ride slowly, walk carefully). Present the rule on the slide: an adjective describes a thing or place (often after is/was); an adverb says how we do something. Spelling: -ly, y → -ily; irregular good → well, fast, hard. Concept check: a quiet street / speak quietly. PM slide 2 12:45 (15) Choose the right word: learners come to the board in turn and click. The class says why: does it describe a thing, or how someone does it? Note: hardly is not the adverb of hard. Slide 3 13:00 (20) PCs, on their own: Find the error – tap the mistake, then type the correct sentence (20 sentences). Walk round and note the most common mistakes for feedback. Slide 4 · Find the error page 13:20 (20) PCs, online maps: each learner searches for their morning place on Google Maps and finds the nearest station, the opening times (if any), the walking time from college and two adjectives from reviews; then one thing that is the same as the text and one new thing. Quick class share. Slide 5 · Google Maps 13:40 (25) Write and post: 4–5 sentences about a favourite place in London with three adjectives and one adverb, posted in Teams General. Then each learner reads two posts and replies with one question, and answers the questions they get. Show two posts on the screen: praise good adjectives and correct one adjective/adverb mistake together. Slides 6–7 · Teams 14:05 (20) Who Wants to Be a Millionaire, whole class and teacher-led: learners leave the PCs and face the screen. Click the button on slide 8 – the game opens with today’s 15 questions loaded. You run it on the projector: read each question aloud, the whole class holds up A–D on the Vote card (QR on the slide), and you click the class’s answer. Slide 8 · Millionaire game 14:25 (5) Before you go: pairs say sentences with quiet/quietly and good/well, and finish “Next time I read a new word, I will …”. Slide 9
e3/reading/docs/student-services-email.p: Entry 3 Reading: Student Services Email Name: ______________________ Date: ______________ Read the email and answer the questions. Dear Colleagues, I hope you are well. As I will be visiting your Adult ESOL classes next week, I wanted to send you my short Student Services presentation in advance. It would be really helpful if you could have the presentation open or ready on the classroom computer when I arrive. This means you won’t need to log out for me to log in, and we can get started straight away without taking unnecessary time out of your lesson. Thank you very much for your support. I look forward to seeing you and your students next week. Kind regards, Questions 1. Who is this email for? Circle one. A. ESOL learners B. ESOL teachers C. Student Services staff D. A college manager 2. What is the main purpose of the email? Circle one. A. To invite teachers to a meeting B. To ask teachers to give a talk C. To tell teachers she is coming and ask them to prepare something D. To show teachers how to use the PCs 3. When is the writer coming to the groups? 4. What has the writer shared with this email? Circle one. A. A timetable B. Some slides about Student Services C. A list of learners’ names D. A letter for learners to take home 5. What does the writer want teachers to do before she gets there? Circle one. A. Turn off the PC B. Print copies for the group C. Have her slides showing on the screen D. Sign out of their account 6. Why does she want this? Circle one. A. She does not have a password. B. The PCs in the rooms are slow. C. She wants the group to lose as few minutes as possible. D. The learners need the PC for their work. 7. True or False? Write T or F. The writer’s talk will be long. ______ b) Without the slides ready, the teacher would have to sign out of the PC. ______ c) The writer is grateful for the teachers’ help. ______ d) The writer hopes to meet the learners as well as the teachers. ______ 8. Find a word or phrase in the email that means: before (paragraph 2): ________________ b) immediately (paragraph 3): ________________ c) not needed (paragraph 3): ________________ Entry 3 Reading: Student Services Email – Answers Answer Key B C Next week B C C F b) T c) T d) T in advance b) straight away c) unnecessary

e3/reading/docs/hackney-places-jigsaw-re: E3 Reading – Hackney Places – Group A Ridley Road Market 1 Ridley Road Market is in Dalston, a short walk from Dalston Kingsland station. It is one of the oldest street markets in Hackney. Every morning, traders set up their stalls along the narrow street. 2 You can buy fresh fruit and vegetables, fish, meat, colourful fabrics and cheap things for the kitchen. Many stalls sell food from Africa, the Caribbean and Turkey, so it is a good place to find ingredients from home. 3 The market is busy and noisy. Traders shout loudly to tell people about their prices, and music comes from some of the shops. Prices are usually lower than in the supermarket, especially at the end of the day, when traders want to sell everything quickly. 4 Bring cash, because some small stalls do not take cards. Go early if you want the best fish. Walk carefully when it rains – the ground can be slippery. You are the expert for this place. 1 Read the text alone. 2 On your question sheet, answer the questions for your place only. 3 Underline the words in the text that prove each answer. Write the question number next to them. 4 Check with your group. Keep this text: in your new group, read your underlined words aloud to prove your answers. Don’t show the text. E3 Reading – Hackney Places – Group B London Fields and the Lido 1 London Fields is a large green park between Hackney Central and Broadway Market. On sunny days it is full of people. Families have picnics on the grass, children play happily in the playground, and friends play football or table tennis. There is also a special area where you can have a barbecue. 2 At one side of the park is London Fields Lido, an outdoor swimming pool. It is 50 metres long and the water is heated, so people swim there all year – even in December! The lido is not free, and on busy days it is a good idea to book online. If you are not a strong swimmer, use the slow lane and swim calmly. 3 The park is free and open every day. In winter it gets dark early, so walk home with a friend in the evening. You are the expert for this place. 1 Read the text alone. 2 On your question sheet, answer the questions for your place only. 3 Underline the words in the text that prove each answer. Write the question number next to them. 4 Check with your group. Keep this text: in your new group, read your underlined words aloud to prove your answers. Don’t show the text. E3 Reading – Hackney Places – Group C Broadway Market 1 Broadway Market is a street near London Fields and the Regent’s Canal. During the week it is a quiet street with small shops, cafés and a bookshop. But every Saturday and Sunday it changes completely. More than a hundred stalls fill the road, and thousands of people come from all over London. 2 The weekend market is famous for food. You can buy fresh bread, cheese, cakes and flowers, or eat hot food from many different countries. The food is delicious, but it is often expensive – a coffee and a cake can cost eight or nine pounds. If you want to save money, walk slowly along the street first and look at all the prices before you buy. 3 The market gets very crowded after eleven o’clock, so try to arrive early. It is a nice walk from London Fields, and you can sit by the canal to eat. You are the expert for this place. 1 Read the text alone. 2 On your question sheet, answer the questions for your place only. 3 Underline the words in the text that prove each answer. Write the question number next to them. 4 Check with your group. Keep this text: in your new group, read your underlined words aloud to prove your answers. Don’t show the text. E3 Reading – Hackney Places – Group D The Regent’s Canal 1 The Regent’s Canal runs through Hackney, past Broadway Market and Victoria Park. Next to the water there is a path, called the towpath, where you can walk or ride a bike. It is free and open all the time, and it is one of the most peaceful places in the borough. 2 On the canal you will see narrowboats – long, thin boats painted in bright colours. Some people live on these boats all year. You will also see ducks, swans and sometimes a heron standing very still in the water. 3 The towpath is narrow, so be polite. Cyclists should ride slowly and ring their bell when they come up behind people. Walkers should keep to one side. Do not feed bread to the ducks – it is bad for them. On a sunny afternoon, it is lovely to walk all the way from Hackney to Islington. You are the expert for this place. 1 Read the text alone. 2 On your question sheet, answer the questions for your place only. 3 Underline the words in the text that prove each answer. Write the question number next to them. 4 Check with your group. Keep this text: in your new group, read your underlined words aloud to prove your answers. Don’t show the text.
e3/reading/graffiti-news-error-hunt.html: E3 Mixed Tenses – Graffiti News – Error Hunt Error hunt: this article has 11 grammar mistakes . Click on each wrong word or words. 0 / 11 Show answers Start again The Hackney Bugle Wednesday 21 October 2026 · Your local news Home News Hackney Dalston Homerton What's on Sport Well Street · Local news Angry shop owner tells graffiti artist: "This is my last warning" A poster on a Well Street shutter has got people talking. Is it a warning or a threat? By Bugle reporter · 21 October 2026 · 3 min read The poster on the shutter. It shows two photos from the shop's CCTV camera. Well done! You found all 11 mistakes. A shop owner on Well Street [[have put|has put]] an angry poster on his shutter after graffiti artists [[paint|have painted]] his shop five times this year. The poster, which [[has appeared|appeared]] last week, says "This is my last and final warning". It also shows two photos from the shop's CCTV camera. "I [[have clean|have cleaned]] the shutter many times," the owner told the Bugle. "Last month I [[have paid|paid]] £200 to clean it. I [[am work|work]] every day and I [[doesn't want|don't want]] any trouble." Local people [[has|have]] different opinions. We will read it, find four tenses, and correct the writer's mistakes. Present simple · Present perfect · Past simple · Future with will Talk to your partner Look at the photo Where is this poster? Who wrote it? Who is it for? How does the writer feel? Is there graffiti near your home? Is graffiti art or a crime? Click the photo to make it bigger. Task 1 · Vocabulary Match the words 0 / 10 graffiti vandalise property a warning a threat a promise CCTV watch your back teach someone a lesson pay for your actions something you own, e.g. a house or shop be careful – someone wants to hurt you cameras that film the street or a shop words or pictures painted on a wall be punished for what you did saying "I will hurt you" damage something on purpose telling someone about danger, so they can stop saying "I will do it" – and you really will punish someone so they don't do it again Start again Read the poster · the mistakes are the writer's To the graffiti artist This is my last and final warning I have warned you many time not to graffiti this shop You didn't take my notes seriously. The government & your parents didn't teach you that vandalising someone property is a crime. Now I will have to teach you a lesson not to mess with the wrong person/people I don't make threats, threat is a crime. I make promises, now you will pay for your actions. Yours truly · The Punisher [CCTV photos: 24-09-2026, Thursday, 00:49] Watch your back, sleep with one eye open ********!!!! I have locked on to you, don't say I didn't warned you. Ask yourself, what it worth it???? Task 2 · Reading True, False or Not Given? 0 / 6 1. Before this poster, the writer told the artist to stop. T F NG 2. The writer is calm and friendly. T F NG 3. The camera photos were taken at night. T F NG 4. The writer knows the artist's name. T F NG 5. The writer says it is legal to frighten people. T F NG 6. The writer has spoken to the police. T F NG Task 2 · Reading Answer the questions What did the writer leave for the artist before this poster? Show answer notes Who, says the writer, should have explained the law to the artist? Show answer the government and the artist's parents What day of the week was the artist filmed? Show answer Thursday (24 September 2026) Why does the writer call himself "The Punisher"? Ideas He wants to punish the artist. He wants to sound tough and frightening. Task 3 · Grammar Which tense? Click a sentence, then a box 0 / 9 This is my last and final warning. I have warned you many times. You didn't take my notes seriously. I will have to teach you a lesson. I don't make threats. I have locked on to you. Your parents didn't teach you. You will pay for your actions. I make promises. Present simple I make / I don't make Present perfect I have + past participle Past simple I warned / I didn't warn Future I will + verb Task 3 · Why do we use it? Four tenses on one poster Present simple This is my last warning. I don't make threats. Why? Facts, things that are always true, habits. Present perfect I have warned you many times. Why? Past actions with a result now. We don't say when. Past simple You didn't take my notes seriously. Why? Finished actions in the past. Future (will) You will pay for your actions. Why? Promises, decisions, predictions. Check Think about it "I have warned you many times." Do we know when? Answer No. Is it important now? Answer Yes – this is the last warning. "You didn't take my notes seriously." Is it finished? Answer Yes. "You will pay for your actions." Now or later? Answer Later. Is it a threat or a promise? Discuss He says "promise" – but it is a threat! Task 4 · Find the mistakes Click the wrong word 0 / 5 1 I have warned you many time. 2 Vandalising someone property is a crime. 3 Threat is a crime. 4 Don't say I didn't warned you. 5 Ask yourself, what it worth it? Bonus: "my last and final warning" – what is the problem? Answer last and final mean the same. Use one. Our CCTV 7 (record) the street 24 hours a day. Thank you – we 8 (see) you soon in the shop! Check Show answers Clear Tip: this year isn't finished. Tell the officer: how long it has happened how many times what you did last time what you will do now Student B Police officer What's the problem? How long have you had this problem?
