e3/reading/docs/camping-advice-email-mod: E3 Reading and Writing – Camping Advice Email – Modal Verbs Name: ______________________________ Date: ______________ Task 1 – Read the email From: sarah.khan@email.com To: mike.james@email.com Subject: Help – first camping trip! Hi Mike, I hope you’re well. I’m writing because I need your advice. Next month, I want to go camping for the first time with my family. We have never camped before, and I’m worried about many things. First, I don’t know where to go. Should we camp in the Lake District or near London? We must choose a place that is not too far from home, because my children are young. We don’t need to go far – maybe two hours by car. I could book a campsite with facilities, or we could camp in the countryside. I’m worried because we can’t camp everywhere in the UK. Do you know the rules? Second, what should we take? I know we must have a tent and sleeping bags. But what else do we need? We could buy an expensive camping stove, but we could also cook on a fire. My husband thinks we can use our kitchen table for eating! I think he might be joking. Third, I’m worried about the weather. It can be very cold at night in the UK. We should bring warm clothes – I agree with my husband on that. Do you think we should go in summer? We must avoid the winter, I think. Please help! Can you suggest a good place for camping? Should I buy new equipment? What time of year is best? Best wishes, Sarah 1. Sarah is worried about three things. What are they? 1 ___________________________ 2 ___________________________ 3 ___________________________ 2. Does Sarah want to camp far from London? Why or why not? 3. What does Sarah think her husband is joking about? 4. Find and underline six modal verbs in the email (for example: should, must, could, can’t, might). Task 2 – Write a reply You are Mike. Write a reply to Sarah. Give her advice about camping. Write 8–10 sentences. Where to camp (the Lake District or near London) What equipment to buy or take The best time of year to go Use modal verbs: can, can’t, should, must, could, might. To: sarah.khan@email.com Subject: Re: Help – first camping trip! Hi Sarah, Best wishes, Mike Check your writing: ☐ I used modal verbs correctly ☐ My sentences start with a capital letter and end with a full stop ☐ I answered all three questions ☐ My email makes sense E3 Reading and Writing – Camping Advice Email – Answers (teacher) Teacher copy. Do not hand out. 1. Any three: where to go / the camping rules (where you can camp); what to take (equipment); the weather (cold nights). 2. No. Her children are young, so the place must not be too far from home – about two hours by car. 3. Using their kitchen table for eating on the trip. 4. Any six: should, must, could, can’t, can, might (e.g. Should we camp…, We must choose…, I could book…, we can’t camp everywhere, we can use…, he might be joking). Task 2 – model reply (one example) Hi Sarah, Thanks for your email. I think you should camp near London, because the children are young and it is a shorter journey. You could try a campsite in Essex or Kent. You must book a campsite with toilets and showers – you can’t camp anywhere you like in England. You should take a tent, sleeping bags and a torch. You don’t need to buy an expensive stove; a small gas stove is fine. Your husband might be joking about the table, but a folding table could be useful! You should go in July or August, because the nights are warmer. You must bring warm clothes, because it can still be cold at night. Best wishes, Mike

ESOL Entry 3 Reading — Practice Exam Topic: Learning languages with your ears Name: ________________________ Date: ________________ Time: 1 hour Total: 24 marks Read each text carefully, then answer the questions after it. Answer all the questions. Text 1 — News article 1. What is the main purpose of this article? (1 mark) A to advertise English classes B to report on research about language learning C to tell the life story of a Japanese student D to explain how to take a listening test 2. According to most people, what is the key to improving in a new language? Write one word. (1 mark) 3. Read the sentences. Are they true, false or not given? (3 marks) 4. Why can some English words be difficult for Japanese speakers? (1 mark) A They are very long words. B Japanese has nothing similar to these two sounds. C They are spelled in the same way. D Japanese people never use English words. 5. Which two English words might a Japanese speaker mix up? (Paragraph 3) (1 mark) 6. In paragraph 4, what does “a good ear” mean? (1 mark) A having very clean ears B being able to notice tiny differences in sounds C enjoying listening to music D being good at English grammar Text 2 — Report 7. How many learners did the tests on the internet? (1 mark) 8. In Test 1, what did the students have to do? (1 mark) A copy the sounds out loud B pick out the tone that was slightly higher C write down the words they heard D name the musical instrument 9. What happened each time a learner gave a correct answer? (1 mark) A The test stopped. B It became more difficult to hear the difference. C They won extra points. D The sounds became louder. 10. Read the sentences. Are they true, false or not given? (2 marks) 11. Apart from having a good ear, which two experiences made a difference? (2 marks) 12. In which city did the second group take the tests? (1 mark) 13. Why do the researchers think some learners hear the new vowel as a Japanese one? (1 mark) A They were not paying attention. B They imagine pronouncing it the Japanese way. C The machine was too noisy. D They did not understand the instructions. Text 3 — Email 14. Why did Maria write this email? (1 mark) A to complain about his class B to share some news and give him advice C to invite him to a party D to ask him for help with a study 15. Which organisation does the lead scientist work for? (1 mark) 16. Read the sentences. Are they true, false or not given? (3 marks) 17. Why are the results not certain yet? Give one reason. (1 mark) 18. According to Maria, what should you focus on when you hear the sentence a second time? (1 mark) 19. On which day and at what time does the club meet? (1 mark) End of exam Is a good ear the secret to learning a language? Why do some people learn a new language more quickly than others? Most people think the answer is practice. If you go to more classes, listen more and talk to more people, you will get better. But a new study says this is not the whole story. Researchers from University College London (UCL) and Tohoku University in Japan worked together on the study. They wanted to find out why two people can study for the same number of hours but still hear a language very differently. The researchers looked at Japanese university students who were learning English. They chose two English vowel sounds: the “a” in “cat” and the “u” in “cup”. These sounds do not exist in Japanese. Many Japanese speakers hear the vowel in “cup” as a Japanese “a”, so “cup” and “cap” can sound almost the same to them. The study found that students with a “good ear” – people who can hear very small differences between sounds – were better at hearing the difference between the two English vowels. The results were published in October 2026. Write a tick (✓) in the correct box. True False Not given 3a. The research was a joint project between Britain and Japan. 3b. Everyone who took part was a child. 3c. The learners had been studying English for five years. How the study worked Test 1: Sounds that are not words 140 students from universities in Tokyo did two short tests online. They wore headphones. In the first test, they heard three buzzing sounds. The sounds were not like a human voice. One sound was a little higher than the other two, and the students had to choose it. Each time a student got the answer right, the next sounds were closer together and harder to tell apart. Test 2: English words In the second test, students heard English words, for example “mad” and “mud”. They had to say which word they heard. Native British English speakers got almost every word right. The Japanese students got about 70% right on average, but some did much better than others. Other questions The students also answered questions about their English classes, how often they spoke English, time abroad, pronunciation lessons and music lessons. Studying abroad and pronunciation lessons helped. But a good ear helped about the same amount. The brain scanner A second group of 67 students did the tests at a university in Sendai, Japan. They lay in a brain scanner for about 20 minutes. Students with a weaker ear used the part of the brain that controls speaking more. The researchers think these students may “say” the new sound in their head in a Japanese way, so it sounds like a Japanese sound. Write a tick (✓) in the correct box. True False Not given 10a. People who grew up speaking English in Britain made very few mistakes. 10b. The Japanese learners all had similar results. From: Maria Lopez (ESOL teacher) To: Bich Subject: Train your ears! Hi Bich, Last week I read about a new study from London and Japan. It says that a “good ear” can help you learn a new language. The main researcher, Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, works at the UCL Institute of Education in London. He says that language teaching is often just about “more practice”. He thinks teachers should also help learners to listen carefully to small differences in sounds. He says that playing a musical instrument may help, because musicians practise hearing small changes in sound all the time. However, in this study, music lessons on their own did not make students better at hearing the English vowels. We need to be careful with the results. The study only looked at listening, not speaking. Also, all the students were Japanese, so we don’t know yet if it is the same for speakers of other languages. Here are my tips: Choose one short sentence – from a podcast, a video or the radio. Listen once for the meaning. Listen again, but this time forget the meaning. Just listen to the sounds. Try pairs of words like “ship” and “sheep”, or “full” and “fool”. Practise on the bus to Dalston or while you cook dinner – ten minutes a day is enough. Our free Listening Club starts next week. It’s every Wednesday at 4pm in Room 12, next to the library. Everyone is welcome! Best wishes, Maria Write a tick (✓) in the correct box. True False Not given 16a. The researcher believes learners just need to spend more time studying. 16b. Learners with musical training did better in the listening tests. 16c. Maria plays an instrument.

E3 Reading – Freecycle Name: ________________ Date: __________ Read the text. Then answer the questions. Questions Circle A, B, C or D unless the question tells you to do something else. Freecycle Do you have things at home that you do not need? Maybe an old chair, a lamp or some children’s books? Do not throw them away. You can give them to someone on Freecycle. Freecycle is a website. People use it to give away things for free. Nobody pays any money. There are small groups for different areas. In London, there is a group for almost every area, including Hackney. It is easy to use. First, you join your local group online. Then you write a short message about your item. For example: “Offer: small table, good condition, Mare Street.” People who want the item send you a reply. Usually, the first person to reply gets it. Then they come to your home and collect it. You can also ask for things. If you need a cooker or a winter coat, you can post a message and wait. Freecycle is good for the environment, because less rubbish goes into the ground. It is also good for people. You can get useful things without spending money, and you can help your neighbours. Many people say it feels good to give. 1. e3/reading/too-cold-to-learn-exam-practi: Too Cold to Learn Reading Exam Too Cold to Learn: Reading Practice Entry 3 Reading · exam practice · 2 tasks · 14 questions 40:00 ▶ Before you start This is like the real exam: read the texts and answer the questions. You have 40 minutes for both tasks. Click the timer to start. Read the questions first Then you know what to look for when you read the text. Who is "they" / "she"? Read the sentence before . The answer is usually a person or thing just before the word. What does … mean? Find the word in the text. Read the whole sentence. Try each answer in its place. "This text…" Ask: is it news (reports), an advert (advertises), an invitation (invites), or help (advises)? Write 2 things Write two different answers. Short answers are fine. Alphabetical order Same first letter? Look at the second letter. Then the third. Start Task 1 → Task 1 Read the text and answer questions 1–7. College News Too cold to learn? A survey of 120 students shows that most of them are unhappy about the heating at the college. Eight out of ten students said that their classroom was too cold in October. The heating system is more than 30 years old. It often stops working early in the morning, when the building is coldest. Last week, the temperature in one classroom was only 14°C. "We sit in our coats and scarves all day," says Maria, an ESOL student. "My hands are so cold that I can't write properly. Some of my classmates have stopped coming to class because they keep getting ill." Teachers are also worried. They say that students find it hard to concentrate, and fewer people come to lessons on very cold days. The survey also asked students what helps. Many bring a hot drink to class. Others try to sit near the radiators, but these are often cold too. The college manager, Mr Patel, says the college will put in a new heating system in the spring. Until then, there will be electric heaters in some of the coldest rooms. He has asked students to tell reception if their classroom is cold. "We want everyone to feel comfortable when they are learning," he says. Many students say this is not enough. They want the college to repair the heating now, before the winter begins. ← Back Task 2 → Task 2 Read Text A and Text B. Answer questions 8–14. A Cold classroom – Room 12 To: Mr Patel Dear Mr Patel, I am an ESOL student and I study in Room 12 on Mondays and Wednesdays. I am writing because our classroom has been very cold since the end of October. Most of us wear our coats during the lesson. Last Monday it was so cold that two students went home early. It is very difficult to learn in these conditions. I read in the college newsletter that the heating will be repaired in the spring. However, the spring is a long time away. Could you please put an electric heater in Room 12 as soon as possible? I look forward to hearing from you. Yours sincerely, Ahmed Hassan B Re: Cold classroom – Room 12 To: Ahmed Hassan Dear Ahmed, Thank you for your email. I am sorry to hear about the problems in Room 12. I have asked the site team to check the heating in your room this week. We also have two electric heaters, and one of them will be in Room 12 from Thursday. If the room is still cold after that, please tell your teacher or speak to Linda at reception. She will send me a message. Thank you for letting us know. Kind regards, Raj Patel College Manager ← Task 1 Check my answers → Your results Go back to Task 1 and Task 2. Each question now shows the answer. Click Show in text to see where the answer is. e3/reading/docs/exam-question-types-sort: What Does It Test? Reading Exam Sort Oct 14, 2026 · @Atin Instructions Read the leaflet. Then look at the 21 exam questions. Do not answer them yet. Decide what each question tests and write its number in the sorting grid. There are 3 questions for each skill. The 7 skills Alphabetical order – putting words or names in A–Z order, like a dictionary or a list. Vocabulary – knowing what a word or phrase means. Scanning for information – finding one fact quickly: a time, a date, a number. Understanding the whole text (gist) – the main idea, the purpose, who the text is for. Grammar and punctuation – verb forms, modal verbs, capital letters, full stops, question marks. Text type and layout – what kind of text it is; headings, bullet points, sections. Reading between the lines (inference) – working out something the text does not say directly. Extra task: When you finish sorting, answer the questions. The text HACKNEY WINTER HELP DAY Saturday 7 November, 10am – 3pm Clapton Community Hall, Lower Clapton Road, Hackney Are you new to Hackney? Do you need help or advice this winter? Come to our free Winter Help Day. Everyone is welcome. What can you do? Get a warm coat or boots for adults and children. Talk to a nurse about flu jabs. Get advice about doctors, schools and housing. Join a free English class for beginners at 11am. Lunch There is hot soup and bread from 12 to 1pm. It’s free! Please bring your own bag for clothes. Children must stay with an adult. Last year more than 300 people came. Don’t miss it! For more information, call Amina on 020 7946 0381 or email help@hackneywinter.org.uk The questions What time does the event finish? Choose the correct word: “Last year, Amina ______ the Help Day too.” a) organise b) organises c) organised d) organising Which word comes first in a dictionary? a) clothes b) coat c) children d) class What is the main purpose of this text? a) to sell winter clothes b) to invite people to a free event with help and advice c) to advertise a college English course d) to report on last year’s event Why does the writer use bullet points (•)? a) to list the different things you can do there b) to show the start and finish times c) to give the contact details d) to tell a story In the text, “advice” means: a) money b) a doctor c) information about what you should do d) a form to fill in Why do you think the event is in November? a) The weather is getting cold. b) Children are on holiday. c) The hall is cheaper. d) It is a national holiday. These words are from the text. Put them in alphabetical order: soup, advice, nurse, coat When can people eat? a) 10–11am b) 11am–12 c) midday–1pm d) 1–3pm Rewrite this sentence with the correct capital letters and punctuation: the event is at clapton community hall on saturday What type of text is this? a) a letter b) a leaflet c) a story d) a menu Find a word in the text for something you wear on your feet. Who is this text mainly for? a) teachers b) nurses c) people who have recently moved to the area d) shop owners Can a 10-year-old come to the event alone? Yes or No? How do you know? Here are the names of four helpers. Put them in alphabetical order: Yusuf, Amina, Kofi, Dariusz What number can you ring to find out more? “Children must stay with an adult.” Which word tells you this is a rule? e3/reading/docs/extra-camping-group-mock: E3 Reading – The Camping Group – Mock Reading Paper Name: ______________________________ Date: ______________ Score: ___ / 18 Time: 60 minutes. Read each text, then answer the questions. Task 1 – The Camping Group Read the text and answer questions 1–9. A group of men has been camping together for nearly thirty years. The group started in the mid-1990s and goes camping almost every year. About twelve men are regular members, though the number changes sometimes. They visit different parts of the UK. Atin has been part of the group for ten years and rarely misses a trip. The men enjoy long walks in the countryside. Walks are often between five and fifteen miles. They walk up mountains and along country paths. The walks are not technically difficult, but they are quite challenging because of their length. The men usually complete their walks and then go to a local pub for rest and food. At the pubs, the men drink beer and eat lunch or dinner. They stay for several hours and play cards. The pubs are always different because the group visits different places. The men enjoy spending time together and having silly conversations about football. Sometimes they eat at the campsite instead of a pub. For Atin, the main appeal is the countryside and nature. He enjoys waking up in nature, away from the city. He also values the friendship and the chance to let his hair down with his friends. Most years he feels tired before the trip, but he is usually glad he went when he returns home. The group usually chooses places with good campsites. These are important for the group’s comfort and enjoyment. A good campsite with peace and quiet makes the experience special. 1. When did the camping group start? A In the 1980s B In the mid-1990s C In the early 2000s D In 2015 2. What makes the walks challenging? A They involve steep mountain climbs B They are long, but not very difficult C The weather is always bad D The paths are poorly marked 3. Why do they go to pubs after their walks? A To shelter from bad weather B To rest and have a meal C To meet other walkers D To get directions 4. Put these events in order. Number 1 has been done for you. __1__ The men walk in the countryside _____ They play cards _____ They go to a pub _____ They have something to eat and drink 5. What does “let his hair down” mean? A Cut his hair short B Relax and enjoy himself C Wash his hair D Take off his hat 6. The text is mainly about A how to plan a camping trip B a long-running group and why it matters to them C the best campsites in the UK D why walking is good for your health 7. Write these words in alphabetical order. camping country caravan challenging card 1 ______________ 2 ______________ 3 ______________ 4 ______________ 5 ______________ 8. Why does Atin rarely miss a trip? A He lives closest to the campsites B He has no other hobbies C The trips matter to him, even when he is tired D He organises the trips 9. What does the last paragraph tell you about how the group chooses campsites? A They choose the cheapest sites B They choose sites that are comfortable and quiet C They choose sites at random D They only camp in the mountains Task 2 – The Festival Campsite Read the text and answer questions 10–18. This year, the camping group went to a new place. They arrived on Friday afternoon and put up their tents at the campsite. The walk on Saturday was good and they all enjoyed the countryside. They went to a pub in the evening, had a drink and played cards until late. When they got back to the campsite that night, Atin realised there was a problem. The campsite had changed. It was now a trendy place for young people who wanted to party. There was loud music and noise until the early morning. This was very different from what the group wanted. They prefer peace and quiet in nature. The campsite had other problems too. There were only portaloos, which are small portable toilets. Atin does not like these. They are uncomfortable and not pleasant. The whole place felt like a small music festival, not a peaceful camping trip. The group still tried to enjoy the weekend. The walks were beautiful and the countryside was lovely. The men played cards, talked and ate together. However, Atin felt frustrated. For him, the special part of camping is waking up in nature, with peace and quiet. This campsite did not offer that. He was not as happy with this trip as he usually is. Next year, the group will need to find a better campsite. The place and its facilities are very important to the group’s enjoyment. 10. What is a portaloo? A A toilet in a pub B A small portable toilet C A luxury bathroom D A shower block 11. How did Atin feel about the portaloos? A He thought they were modern B He found them unpleasant C He preferred them to normal toilets D He wanted to use them more 12. Which sentence about the Saturday walk is true? A The group found it boring B The group enjoyed the countryside C The group decided to leave early D The group played cards instead 13. Put these events in order. Number 1 has been done for you. __1__ The group arrives on Friday afternoon _____ Atin realises the campsite has changed _____ They go for a walk _____ They go to a pub in the evening 14. What is most important to Atin about camping? A Playing cards with friends B Going to pubs C Being in nature, with peace and quiet D Getting exercise 15. The text is mainly about A how to choose a good campsite B how a noisy campsite spoiled the group’s weekend C why young people like festivals D why portaloos are uncomfortable 16. Write these words in alphabetical order. weekend walk when would weather 1 ______________ 2 ______________ 3 ______________ 4 ______________ 5 ______________ 17. What did the group still do, despite the problems? A They complained to the owners B They walked, played cards and spent time together C They went home early D They stopped eating together 18. What will the group probably do next year? A Stop camping B Go back to the same campsite C Keep camping, but choose a better campsite D Ask for the campsite to be closed E3 Reading – The Camping Group – Mock Reading Paper – Answers (teacher) Teacher copy. Do not hand out. Alphabetical order tips: Q7 – all start with c: look at the second letter (a, a, a, h, o), then the third and fourth (cam-, cara-, card). Q16 – all start with w: wa, we, we, wh, wo; then weather (wea) comes before weekend (wee). e3/reading/purpose-pronouns-word-meaning: E3 Reading – Purpose, Pronouns & Word Meaning – Projector Lesson E3 Reading · Week 8 · Exam skills Reading detectives Today: why was a text written? What is each part about? Who is “he”? What does a new word mean? Find the clue. Prove the answer. Why was it written? Choose the purpose, then find the clues. 0 / 6 Six purposes, six kinds of clue warn danger · beware · do not · be careful advise you should · it is a good idea to · try to instruct sentences start with a verb: Press… Open… Wait… advertise prices · free · new · best · sale · buy inform facts: dates, times, places · will open / will close describe adjectives · there is / there are · it has In the exam, one question always asks this. Choose the verb that fits the whole text . What is it mainly about? Read the title . Read the first sentence of each paragraph. Stop. Say the topic in four words or fewer . Then read everything to check. The trap: a true detail is not the main point True, but only a detail “The shops used to throw food away.” The main point “A free weekly dinner run by local people.” Ask: does this answer cover the whole text , or just one sentence? Who is “he”? What is “it”? Rosa has a brother . He lives in Leeds. She visits him every month. Look back , not forward. One or more than one? (it / they) A person or a thing? (he, she / it) Follow the arrow 0 / 5 What does the word in bold mean? A new word? Read around it Read the sentence before and after . Good or bad? A thing, a person or an action? Try each answer in the sentence. Does it make sense? No dictionary in the exam. The text gives you the clues. Guess the word 0 / 4 Same idea, different words 0 / 6 Exam questions rarely copy the text. Tap a phrase on the left, then its partner on the right. Kahoot! kahoot.it Enter the game PIN on the screen Teacher: open the Kahoot and press Start (20 questions) Before you go Finish the sentence with your partner “When I do not know a word in the exam, I will …” “When a question asks why a text was written, I will …” ← →

e3/reading/docs/exam-question-words-refe: 4 kinds of reading question Oct 8, 2026 · @Atin There are 4 kinds of reading question. First, read the question. What kind is it? Then you know what to do in the text. Exam words: according to the leaflet = the leaflet says · EXCEPT = but not · mainly = mostly · purpose = the reason for writing · closest in meaning = almost the same meaning · refer to = talk about · probably = very likely · suggest = show, but not say Writing your answer: "(2 marks)" = write 2 different things. "In your own words" = don't copy from the text. Picture Kind of question What to do Exam questions like this 1. Find it The answer is in the text. Underline the important word in the question. Look for it in the text. The answer is near it. True or false? Is it the same as the text? "NOT" and "EXCEPT": find the one answer that is wrong. What time does the library open on Saturday? / According to the leaflet, where can you park? / True or false: the market opens on Sundays. / Which of these is NOT free? 2. Big picture Think about all of the text, not one small part. Look at the heading and the pictures. What is the text mainly about? / Why did Sara write this email? / Who is this leaflet for? / What is the purpose of this notice? 3. Word meaning Read the sentence with the word in it. Try your answer in the sentence. Does it make sense? Small words like it, they and there go back to something before. Find a word in paragraph 2 that means "big". / Which word is closest in meaning to "cheap"? / In line 4, what does "it" refer to? 4. Work it out The answer is not in the words of the text. Look for clues, for example feeling words like happy, angry or terrible. Then think. How does the writer feel about the new bus route? / Where would you probably see this notice? / What does the review suggest about the café?

E3 Mixed Tenses – Graffiti Warning Poster – Reading, Grammar & Error Correction – Teacher notes and answers Teacher notes Entry 3, about 2 hours. Real Hackney shop shutter poster (photo taken October 2026). Project the photo for the lead-in; the worksheet has a typed copy. Aims Recognise and contrast present simple, present perfect, past simple and will future in a real text. Correct common learner errors (all taken from the poster itself). Discuss graffiti, property and threats; write a short notice using all four tenses. Content warning: the original ends with a strong swear word. The worksheet stars it out. Crop or cover the bottom of the photo if you prefer. Stages Discussion point (optional, stronger groups): the writer says “threat is a crime” – then threatens someone. Is this poster legal? What should the shop owner do instead? (Report to the police; use the CCTV as evidence.) Answer key Task 1: 1d, 2g, 3a, 4h, 5f, 6i, 7c, 8b, 9j, 10e Task 2: 1 T · 2 F · 3 T (00:49) · 4 F (signed “The Punisher”) · 5 F (he says a threat is a crime) · 6 F (his parents didn’t teach him) · 7 notes · 8 the government and the artist’s parents · 9 Thursday Task 3 Task 4 many times (plural after many) someone’s property (possessive ’s) A threat is a crime / Threats are crimes (article or plural) I didn’t warn you (base form after didn’t) Is it worth it? (question word order; no what) last and final mean the same – use one Task 5: 1 is · 2 opened · 3 has painted (this year isn’t finished) · 4 paid · 5 don’t want · 6 will report · 7 records · 8 will see Stage Time What happens 1. Lead-in 10 min Show the photo. Pairs: Where is this? Who wrote it? Who is it for? How does the writer feel? Have you seen graffiti in Hackney? Is it art or a crime? 2. Vocabulary 15 min Task 1: match words to meanings. Drill pronunciation: graffiti, vandalise, property, warning, threat, promise. 3. Reading 15 min Task 2: read the typed poster, answer the questions. Check in pairs, then whole class. 4. Grammar noticing 20 min Task 3: find one or more examples of each tense. Board the table. Concept check: I have warned you many times – Do we know when? (No.) Is it important now? (Yes.) You didn’t take my notes seriously – Finished? (Yes.) You will pay – Now or later? (Later.) 5. Error correction 15 min Task 4: the writer made mistakes. Learners find and fix them. Good confidence boost – native speakers make errors too. 6. Controlled practice 15 min Task 5: gap fill – a calmer notice from the same shop. 7. Speaking 15 min Task 6: role play – shop owner tells a police officer what happened. Swap roles. 8. Writing 15 min Task 7: write a polite notice (40–60 words) using all four tenses. Stronger learners: write the graffiti artist’s reply. Tense Examples Use Present simple This is my last warning. I don’t make threats. I make promises. Vandalising property is a crime. Facts, things always true, habits Present perfect I have warned you many times. I have locked on to you. Past action, result now; time not given Past simple You didn’t take my notes seriously. Your parents didn’t teach you… Don’t say I didn’t warn you. Finished actions in the past Future (will) I will have to teach you a lesson. You will pay for your actions. Promises, decisions, predictions

A Banana That Stays Yellow Extra activities: vocabulary, grammar and food waste Read the text. Then do the activities. Activity 1: Words from the text Start with the words from the banana text. Match each word to its meaning. Write the letter. Activity 2: Opposites Now you know these words, learn their opposites. Write the opposite of each word. Use the box. Activity 3: Verbs with two parts Bananas go brown and people throw them away. These verbs are in the text too. Complete the sentences with a verb from the box. 1. Apples ______________ quickly after you cut them. 2. Put the milk in the fridge to ______________ it ______________. 3. Don’t ______________ that old bread. We can make toast with it. 4. He used a big knife to ______________ the melon. 5. The scientists ______________ the part of the DNA that makes bananas brown. (past) Activity 4: Grammar: “When you …” for facts You used verbs like go brown and keep fresh. Now use them to talk about facts. In the text: “When you cut a banana, the inside meets the air.” We use When + present simple, present simple for things that are always true. Match the two halves. Now write 2 sentences of your own about food. When I … Activity 5: Grammar: comparing things So how is the new banana different from a normal one? Let’s compare. In the text: “It stays yellow for much longer.” Complete the sentences with the correct form of the word in brackets. 1. The new banana stays yellow ______________ than a normal banana. (long) 2. A brown banana is ______________ than a yellow banana. (soft) 3. Food in the fridge stays ______________ than food on the table. (fresh) 4. A ripe banana tastes ______________ than a green banana. (sweet) 5. Eating fruit is ______________ for you than eating sweets. (good) Activity 6: Grammar: has / have + past participle The banana story is news. Look at how the news tells us what has happened so far. In the text: “Tropic Biosciences has made a new banana.” News often uses has / have + past participle. Complete the sentences with the verb in brackets. 1. The company ______________ a new banana. (make) 2. The banana ______________ an important test. (pass) 3. Scientists ______________ the banana’s DNA. (change) 4. Many people ______________ about the new banana on the news. (hear) 5. The government ______________ not ______________ yet. (decide) Activity 7: Order: First, Then, After that, Finally The government has not decided yet. So what happens next? How does a new food get to the shops? Put the steps in the correct order. Write the letters. A Shops start to sell it. B Scientists make a new food. C Government ministers make the final decision. D The Food Standards Agency checks that it is safe. Order: ______ ______ ______ ______ Now write the steps as sentences. Use First, Then, After that and Finally. Activity 8: Grammar: can / can’t / must There are rules before a new food can go on sale. Talk about rules and what is possible. Complete each sentence with can, can’t or must. 1. The Food Standards Agency ______________ agree before shops sell the new banana. 2. You ______________ buy the new banana yet. It is not in shops. 3. You ______________ eat a brown banana. It is safe. 4. You ______________ eat food that smells bad. It can make you ill. 5. You ______________ use old bananas to make banana bread. Activity 9: More food words Food that is still good to eat is often thrown away. Here are more words to talk about food at home. Complete the sentences with a word or phrase from the box. 1. This banana is yellow and soft. It is ______________ and ready to eat. 2. Don’t eat that apple! It is brown and smells bad. It is ______________. 3. Check the ______________ on the milk before you drink it. 4. We cooked too much rice last night, so I am eating the ______________ for lunch. 5. We put old fruit and vegetables in the ______________ bin to help our plants grow. Activity 10: Speaking: talk with a partner Now use your new words. Talk about you and your home. Ask and answer the questions. Use the words and grammar from this worksheet. 1. What fruit do you eat every week? 2. What food do you throw away most often? Why? 3. How do you keep food fresh at home? 4. Would you eat the new banana? Why? / Why not? 5. In your country, what do people do with old bananas? Activity 11: Writing: food waste at home Finally, write down your ideas from the speaking. Write 5–6 sentences about food waste in your home. Try to use: When …, can / can’t / must, and one comparing word (for example fresher, better). Example: When I buy too much bread, it goes hard. I can put it in the freezer. Name: Date: A Banana That Stays Yellow Do you hate it when a banana goes brown and soft in your bag? Soon this may not be a problem. A company in Norfolk called Tropic Biosciences has made a new banana. It stays yellow for much longer after you cut it open. The banana has now passed an important test in England. Why do bananas go brown? When you cut a banana, the inside meets the air. This starts a natural change, and the fruit gets darker. A brown banana is not dangerous. You can still eat it. But it does not look nice, so many people throw it away. What is different? Scientists changed the banana’s DNA. They switched off the part that makes it go brown. They did not add anything from other plants or animals. The company says the new banana: • stays fresh for several days in a box in the fridge • stays fresh for up to 24 hours on a kitchen table • will mean much less food waste When can we buy it? l1/reading/docs/freecycle-in-the-uk-read: L1 Reading – Freecycle in the UK Name: ________________ Date: __________ Read the text. Then answer the questions. Questions Circle the correct answer: A, B, C or D. Freecycle in the UK Freecycle is a global online platform where people can give away things they no longer need, instead of throwing them away. The aim is to reduce waste and encourage people to reuse items. Freecycle works through local groups. Members can offer items, or ask for items they are looking for. Freecycle is popular in the UK, and there are groups in most towns and cities. In London, almost every borough has one, including Hackney. Members offer a wide range of items, from furniture and electronics to books and clothing. When an item is listed, anyone in the group can reply to say they are interested. The owner then chooses who will receive it, usually on a first-come, first-served basis. Nothing is sold: every item is free, and the new owner normally collects it. Freecycle helps the environment because less rubbish goes to landfill. It also builds community spirit, as people feel good about helping others. It can save money too, because people can get useful things without paying for them. The process is simple, and anyone with internet access can join. Many people in the UK use Freecycle to declutter their homes while also giving something back to their community. 1. What is the main purpose of Freecycle? A To help people earn money B To cut down on rubbish by passing things on C To sell second-hand goods cheaply D To run an online shop 2. Which statement about how Freecycle is organised is true? A There is one group for the whole country. B Groups are based in particular areas. C Groups only exist in London. D You must meet other members before joining. 3. What does ‘first-come, first-served’ mean? A The person who replies fastest gets the item. B The person who needs it most gets the item. C The owner decides to keep the item. D The item goes to someone chosen at random. 4. How does an item usually reach its new home? A The owner delivers it. B Freecycle posts it. C The person receiving it picks it up. D It is left at a local shop. 5. In the text, what does ‘declutter’ mean? A Arrange things neatly B Add more things to a room C Get rid of things you don’t need D Put things into storage 6. What do you need to take part? A A car B A way to get online C A small fee D A large home 7. What is one personal benefit of Freecycle mentioned in the text? A People can get useful things at no cost. B People can earn extra income. C People get discounts in local shops. D People get free delivery. 8. Which item is NOT given as an example in the text? A Electronics B Shoes C Furniture D Books 9. In the text, ‘landfill’ is… A a recycling centre. B a site where unwanted material is buried. C a warehouse for reusable goods. D a charity collection point. 10. How does Freecycle affect relationships between local people? A It causes arguments between neighbours. B It gives people a sense of belonging and helping each other. C It makes local shops lose business. D It makes people spend more. L1 Reading – Freecycle in the UK – Reading Practice Questions – Answers (teacher) Keep separate from the student handout. 1 B – To cut down on rubbish by passing things on 2 B – Groups are based in particular areas. 3 A – The person who replies fastest gets the item. 4 C – The person receiving it picks it up. 5 C – Get rid of things you don’t need 6 B – A way to get online 7 A – People can get useful things at no cost. 8 B – Shoes (the text says clothing, not shoes) 9 B – a site where unwanted material is buried. 10 B – It gives people a sense of belonging and helping each other.

assessments/speaking-placement-test.html: ESOL Speaking & Listening Placement Interview – teachers only ESOL Speaking & Listening Placement Interview (E1–L2) A spoken placement interview run by Claude. The learner wears headphones and talks to it directly; it ends with an approximate ESB level. ⚠ Teachers only – not for learners This page is not a test learners can sit on their own. Running it needs a teacher with a Claude account, signed in on the classroom machine, with the project open in voice mode. Learners must never open the interview themselves – they would see the questions, the levels and other learners' results. Results and feedback are released only to the teacher, on asking. Vary nothing by hand: the interview changes itself between learners so the next one in the room can't copy answers. Teacher PIN Show instructions Four digits. Ask Atin if you don't have it. Wrong PIN. Try again. How to run it Open the ESOL project in Claude on the classroom machine and turn on voice mode. Open the ESOL project in Claude ↗ Say or type: run the speaking placement test Put headphones and a microphone on the first learner. Sit them where the rest of the class can't hear the questions. The learner says Hello, I'm here and the interview begins. It asks one question at a time and lasts about five minutes. It finishes with Thank you, that's the end of the test and asks the learner to fetch the next student. Then it stays quiet until the next learner says Hello, I'm here . No result is read out in front of the learner. To see the results table, say This is the teacher . What it covers Range ESB ESOL Skills for Life, Entry 1 to Level 2+ Length About 5 minutes per learner; it stops early once the level is clear Skills Speaking and listening. One listening text, returned to later with different questions, with a plain spoken explanation before the first listening item Result An approximate level per learner, plus two or three sentences of feedback. Ask for the full breakdown if you want it Records A results table per class, shown in the chat to the teacher on request Before the first learner Test the microphone and headphones. A room where others can overhear defeats the point. Have the class list to hand – each learner gives their name at the start. Give the rest of the class something to get on with: this runs one learner at a time. SMART targets can be generated from the same results in the project afterwards. ← Back to the ESOL Library

all-levels/docs/complaint-email-too-cold: Too Cold to Learn: Complaint Emails All levels (E1–L1) · PC room · about 2 hours · Teacher Plan · Version 2 Lesson page: https://claude.ai/artifact/6w2r2YAcvdrXd1qJV1UCtb Aims Read and compare two complaint emails: polite and factual vs. rude and vague. Recognise formal and polite language. Correct common grammar mistakes in emails. Plan and write a clear, polite complaint email with facts, effects and a request. Check a partner's email. Use Outlook to send a real email (optional) to the college managers about the heating. ESB links: Writing (format, register, paragraphs, accuracy). Reading (purpose, main points, referencing, vocabulary in context). S&L (discussion, giving opinions). Before the lesson Share the lesson page with the class (Teams General channel) and put it on the projector. Upload the Kahoot file (import from spreadsheet). If you can, bring a thermometer: a real reading makes the emails much stronger. Write on the board: To: Katie.Stafford@NCCLondon.ac.uk · Cc: Jennie.Turner@… and Sarah.Wall@… (these are already filled in on the page). Check learners can sign in to Outlook on the web with their college account. Stages Differentiation E1: frame with drop-downs: name, room, clothes, effect. Pair a weaker E1 with a stronger E1 for sign-in and sending. E2: frame with past simple gaps (was / were / wore). Fast finishers move to E3. E3: paragraph prompts with phrase chips; present perfect focus (have been / have stopped). L1: formal register, evidence (HSE: indoor workplaces normally at least 16°C), balance ('I understand… However…'), request with a timescale. Extension: draft a polite follow-up for two weeks' time. Classroom version (no PCs) Use the page on the projector only, and print the Classroom Writing Frames. Print only the levels you need: one side per learner. Warm up, Read, Polite?, Fix: whole class on the projector. You click; learners answer with A–D vote cards or mini whiteboards. Kahoot: on phones, as normal. Write: on the paper frame (1 Our facts, 2 Write). Learners with smartphones can open the page link and use the Write tab instead. Partner check: part 3 on the frame. Send: learners type their email into Outlook on their phone (college account), or send it in their next PC session. Learners with the page on their phone can use the Outlook button. Important: sending is the learners' choice Tell learners clearly: they may send, or just keep their email. They write their own words and use their own names. Don't send on anyone's behalf. Polite, factual emails from many learners are the most effective and the hardest to dismiss. Follow-up (about 2 weeks later) If there's no proper reply, teach an escalation email. Refer to the date of the first emails and the number of complaints, ask again for a date, and Cc Gerry McDonald (Group Principal & CEO). Learners who used the complaints form can quote their complaint.
